#150750. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1677 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, upcoming report shows.
  • Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an crucial purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, upcoming report shows. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an crucial purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

Industry observers note that however, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

Industry observers note that “The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

According to recent reports, jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, noted she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company released and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

It has been revealed that “Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

Sources indicate that mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

Most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic remarked. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

Recent findings suggest that “Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

According to recent reports, however, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt mentioned. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply concerns posed a challenge, forcing it to presently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

“PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

Beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

Recent findings suggest that “Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” mentioned Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

Recent findings suggest that sephora rolled out its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is presently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

In a recent development, the gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a company on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is currently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high reveals the scale of India's climate challenge.

Recent findings suggest that “I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann said. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

And when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, says the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

It has been revealed that “Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability complications) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she stated. “Market leadership is key.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (798 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing new details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System.
  • It has been revealed that upcoming research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed.
  • According to recent reports, the Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing new details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide important clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

It has been revealed that upcoming research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

According to recent reports, the Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Crucial Clues.

Dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

"The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan noted.

Sources indicate that "Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth.".

Sources indicate that "By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment.".

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts.

It has been revealed that to investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

These findings offer a latest perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

In a recent development, the implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth.

"The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan remarked.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a latest era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side.".

It has been revealed that the return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.

Materials provided by Curtin University. Original written by Lucien Wilkinson. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor.
  • Recent findings suggest that the picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek.
  • According to recent reports, the meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor.

Recent findings suggest that the picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic.

According to recent reports, the meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower. The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet, which broke apart in the 1850s.

In a recent development, when Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm. This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour.

Not many stargazers may be be acquainted with the Andromedid meteor shower. What used to be a spectacular annual meteor shower is now hardly even visible.

But in 1885, the Andromedids were an annual treat for skywatchers hoping for a chance to see the remains of Biela's comet (a comet first spotted in 1772 and then found - for the third time - in 1826 by the German astronomer Wilhelm von Biela, from whom it gets its name).

Camera technology has come a long way since 1885, which is good since it is a bit harder to see the Andromedids these days. Instead of photographic plates or digital cameras, astronomers now have to use special tracking equipment to record images of Andromedid meteors.

In 2011, astronomers declared that the meteor shower seemed to be undergoing a resurgence of activity, with 50 meteors per hour, and upticks were expected in 2018 and 2023.

According to recent reports, want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#150743. Industry News: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1163 w)

Industry News: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, upcoming research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas.
  • Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, upcoming research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors. The findings also raise questions about a familiar feature of the Milky Way, suggesting that part of what astronomers have long considered a spiral arm may actually be something else.

Sources indicate that the discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas. These waves squeeze the gas together, creating conditions that allow fresh stars to form in a region where such intense forces usually prevent their birth.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.

Lead author Dr. Hillary Davis, who recently completed her PhD at the University of Sydney's School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy, said the research provides new insights into the structures near the galactic center and how gas moves around them.

It has been revealed that "At its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for fresh stars to be born on a massive scale," Dr. Davis remarked.

Recent findings suggest that "In most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. What's extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed.".

A Hidden Star Factory at the Heart of the Milky Way.

According to recent reports, the Milky Way belongs to a class of galaxies known as barred spiral galaxies. Unlike galaxies with only a central concentration of stars and surrounding spiral arms, these systems contain an elongated structure of stars stretching across their central region. In our galaxy, this structure is called the Galactic bar.

Industry observers note that as the bar rotates, its gravity influences nearby gas, driving it into powerful shock fronts. These fronts compress the gas in much the same way that a shock wave compresses air.

It has been revealed that studying this structure from Earth is particularly difficult because we are located inside the Milky Way rather than viewing it from the outside. Large amounts of cosmic dust also block our view of the galactic center.

"The Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view," Dr. Davis remarked.

"As a result, the bar's properties have been highly debated.".

According to recent reports, observations of other barred galaxies have shown that these shock fronts generally inhibit the formation of new stars, even in regions containing abundant gas. The intense conditions make it difficult for the gas to collapse into stars.

Sources indicate that however, the new findings indicate that the Milky Way may behave differently. Although it is not the only known example, our galaxy appears to belong to a relatively small group in which substantial star formation takes place along the shock fronts of the central bar.

"We believe that the Milky Way's bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies," Dr. Davis said.

A Milky Way Spiral Arm May Not Be What It Seems.

To investigate this unusual activity, the research team compared detailed computer simulations showing how galaxies change over billions of years with astronomical observations of regions where massive stars are forming.

In a recent development, A crucial part of the evidence came from masers, naturally occurring sources that emit highly concentrated microwave radiation. These emissions are associated with the formation of massive stars and operate on a principle similar to lasers, but at microwave wavelengths.

By examining the positions of these masers, the researchers uncovered a striking match between actual observations and the locations of shock fronts predicted by their simulations.

In a recent development, "We found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations," Dr. Davis said. "This suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar.

"This raises questions about the Galaxy's spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation," she said.

The possibility is significant because it suggests that some of the star formation previously attributed to the Norma spiral arm could instead be occurring along the central bar. If confirmed, this interpretation would change how astronomers understand the arrangement of stars and gas in that part of the Milky Way.

Fresh Evidence Could Redraw the Milky Way's Map.

Beyond revealing an unusual location for star birth, the research also sheds light on the physical properties of the Galactic bar itself.

Astronomers have debated the structure's length, orientation, and rotation speed for decades, partly because the Milky Way's dust and our viewing position make direct measurements so challenging.

In a recent development, "Our findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar," Dr. Davis remarked.

Sources indicate that the team's analysis indicates that the bar extends approximately 4.3 kiloparsecs, equivalent to about 14,000 light-years, outward from the galactic center along its long axis. This supports a picture of the Milky Way containing a relatively long bar that rotates slowly.

The results illustrate how increasingly sophisticated simulations can help scientists investigate regions of our galaxy that are difficult to observe directly. By comparing models spanning billions of years with the available astronomical evidence, researchers can narrow down the possible structures and processes shaping the Milky Way.

"By comparing a new generation of large-scale computerized galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way," Dr. Davis noted.

The authors reported no competing interests. Research funding came from the Australian Research Council, the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish National Space Agency, the LMK Foundation and eSSENCE (Sweden).

Computing resources and data storage were provided through National Computing Infrastructure Australia, an NCRIS capability supported by the Australian Government, and LUNARC, the Centre for Scientific and Technical Computing at Lund University, Sweden.

Tech Report: Monica Bellucci on Challenging Hollywood Ageism in James Bond, Working With Mel Gibson and the Power of Onscreen Nudity: ‘It’s Like a Costume That Brings a Role to Life’

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Monica Bellucci, the glamorous Italian star who broke through internationally with “Malena” and “Irreversible,” was 50 when she made James Bond history as the oldest woman to play a Bond girl in Sam Mendes’ “Spectre.”.
  • But rather than marking the twilight of her career as a Hollywood sex symbol, the movie ushered in a new chapter for Bellucci whose career has been enjoying a second wind in recent years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monica Bellucci, the glamorous Italian star who broke through internationally with “Malena” and “Irreversible,” was 50 when she made James Bond history as the oldest woman to play a Bond girl in Sam Mendes’ “Spectre.”.

But rather than marking the twilight of her career as a Hollywood sex symbol, the movie ushered in a new chapter for Bellucci whose career has been enjoying a second wind in recent years. Related Stories Matt Damon Narrates Ford Racing's 'Go Like Hell' Thanksgiving Day Ad Directed by Zack Snyder Danny Boyle Backs Jack O’Connell as a Bond Villain, but Says He ‘Would Have Been Great’ as 007.

In a recent development, during a candid, wide-ranging masterclass moderated by Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival, Bellucci recalled that Mendes really “wanted to show a mature woman, and I thought it was a beautiful idea.” “He told me, ‘Listen, I have a strong and unusual role that’s going to be surprising, a little revolutionary,” she said. “I was 50, and I had never seen a 50-year-old Bond woman. So I think I’m the oldest James Bond woman, lady or girl that we’ve ever seen,” Bellucci said with a laugh in front of a huge crowd of locals and film students who queued for over two hours to get in.

Ultimately, “Spectre” and Emir Kusturica’s “On the Milky Road,” in which she starred opposite the Serbian filmmaker, came at a pivotal moment in her life.

“Suddenly, I had two very strong roles. Those two films helped me get through the transition of turning 50, which wasn’t easy for an actress,” she said.

Sources indicate that bellucci, whose body of work has largely been shaped by celebrated male auteurs — from Francis Ford Coppola to Giuseppe Tornatore, Gaspar Noé and David Lynch — also noted that she has enjoyed working with more female directors in recent years. She cited Alice Rohrwacher with her Cannes-prizewinning “The Wonders,” Rebecca Miller with “The Private Lives of Pippa Lee,” Kaouther Ben Hania with “The Man Who Sold His Skin” and Léa Mysius’ “Birthday Girl,” which competed at this year’s Cannes.

“When I was younger, there weren’t as many female directors as there are today. It’s new to have so many female directors, screenwriters and even technicians on a set, so many women. We’re witnessing something completely new,” she said.

Industry observers note that “It’s another way of telling stories, sometimes another vision. And between women, sometimes there’s this ‘je ne sais quoi,’ as we say in France. Suddenly, we look at each other and, without words, we express ourselves and we understand each other. So I also really like working with women whenever possible.”.

Bellucci remarked the roles she is being offered have also evolved as she’s gotten older, allowing her to explore facets of herself that she couldn’t have accessed earlier in her career.

According to recent reports, “Our body is our working instrument. So the instrument changes and, consequently, the roles change. It’s another part of ourselves that’s expressing itself,” she said. “As we get older, we also gain experience, and we have another way of telling the story of life.”.

Bellucci, who made her debut on stage in 2019 with the solo show “Maria Callas: Letters and Memoirs” — which she toured in different countries and played in French, Italian and English — mentioned she felt lucky that “times have changed and there’s a lot of respect for women in cinema.”.

Recent findings suggest that “In the ’40s, ’50s and ’60s, it was very difficult for a woman over 40 to have a career, even if she was very talented and still had everything it took. And today that has changed.” She cited Susan Sarandon, Judi Dench, Jamie Lee Curtis and Meryl Streep as actors who have paved the way for women to continue playing compelling roles as they age. “There are magnificent actresses who are absolutely fearless,” she remarked, singling out Streep. “She’s so fearless and she’s incredible. There are several actresses who are free in that sense.”Bellucci also reminisced about her defining role in Giuseppe Tornatore’s 2000 drama “Malena,” which earned two Oscar nominations. Bellucci plays a young woman whose beauty triggers desire and eventually violence in a small Sicilian town during World War II.

Bellucci, who notes she was already a film buff from a young age “watching three films a day,” had met the Oscar-winning director of “Cinema Paradiso” during her modeling years in Italy and worked with him on a commercial for Dolce & Gabbana. Four years later, while Bellucci was shooting “Under Suspicion” with Gene Hackman and Morgan Freeman, Tornatore called to offer her the lead role which he wrote for her.

Sources indicate that “The script was already very powerful because it tells the story of women living in a man’s world, the difficulty of those relationships, the violence. It’s about a woman who finds herself alone in a man’s world and has to deal with it. Ultimately, it’s still a very contemporary film,” she noted.

Industry observers note that at the time, Bellucci had already broken through in France with “L’Appartment,” starring opposite Vincent Cassel, and “Malena” represented a daring role which required a great deal of nudity and some intimate scenes with a teenage actor. She stated approached these scenes “very naturally.”.

According to recent reports, “I came from fashion, so I had a freedom with my body that came from the work I had done before,” Bellucci noted. “Even today, I think nudity can serve to bring a character to life. When I see films like ‘Anora’ or ‘Poor Things,’ these are films where the actresses’ bodies are very notable in bringing the characters to life.”.

Sources indicate that “When you play a role, if nudity is part of that role, it’s simply a working tool. It’s not a way of exposing yourself. In fact, it’s like a costume that brings a role to life.”.

During the conversation, Bellucci also talked about her experience shooting Mel Gibson’s highly controversial blockbuster “The Passion of the Christ,” in which she portrayed Mary Magdalene.

“I had another action film at the same time, and I chose ‘The Passion of the Christ’ because I wanted to work with Mel Gibson. I’d seen films of his that I liked, and it was an experience I wanted to have.”.

She noted she had no regrets about making the 2004 biblical epic, which sparked controversy over its graphic violence and portrayal of Jewish figures, and went on to gross over $611 million worldwide.

Sources indicate that “I think every time a film sparks a discussion, it means it was vital to make it. Because discussing and exchanging ideas — that’s the power of cinema,” she said.

Sources indicate that she said she approached the role Mary Magdalene as “a simple, human woman who experiences something greater than herself, something she can’t really explain. There is a form of spirituality in everyone.” Although the film didn’t bring her closer to her Catholic upbringing, she said she felt “there is never anything bad in religions. It’s the political use of religion that is dangerous.”.

Bellucci also praised Gibson for being “really incredible with actors on set” and revealed she had talked to him about the two-part follow up, “The Resurrection of the Christ,” which he’s currently filming. “Yes, we spoke,” she stated of the sequel, adding: “I think he’s a great director.”.

During the masterclass, Bellucci also revisited the memorable scene in “The Matrix Reloaded” in which her character, Persephone, demands that Neo — played by Keanu Reeves — kiss her as if he were kissing Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) in exchange for her help.

In a recent development, asked whether she had to do numerous takes of the kissing scene with Keanu Reeves, Bellucci quipped, “It’s not tiring, is it? You can do it.”.

“He’s someone who is very gentle, respectful. We met on ‘Dracula’ and saw each other again years later on ‘The Matrix,’“ she noted of Reeves.

Despite landing supporting roles in several Hollywood movies at the height of her international breakthrough, Bellucci said she never felt the desire to relocate to the U.S.

“I like America. I love all these possibilities, all this energy, the possibility of making big films as well as independent films. And I like going there. But I feel profoundly European. I live between Paris and Rome, and I love that,” she stated.

“The more time passes, the more I realize that I adore my profession and I still have that passion. But I also love the real things in my life. I love having my friends, I love my family. I also love having a kind of everyday life, something that keeps me connected to something real,” she noted. “I like cinema, but I prefer life.”.

Among her more recent Hollywood outings was Tim Burton’s “Beetlejuice Beetlejuice,” in which she plays Delores, Beetlejuice’s vengeful, soul-sucking ex-wife who comes back from the dead to hunt him down.

Bellucci stated Burton’s drawings of Delores helped her envision the character. “He expresses so many things through his drawings and he had made a magnificent drawing of this character. I was already really inspired by that,” she said.

“With all her scars, Delores is a bit of a parody of existence, a metaphor for life,” she said, adding that the role necessitated three hours of makeup every day. “We all have scars. We have to face them, continue to live with them and move forward.” Speaking of the scene in which she reassembles her body, she said “there were special effects, but it was also a bit like a a macabre dance.”.

Bellucci, who also worked with Ben Hania and Moroccan-Belgian directing duo Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah on “Seven Dogs,” was also upbeat about the new generation of Arab filmmakers.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s a lot happening. This festival is proof of that, isn’t it? All these first and second films, these incredible young filmmakers, beautiful films like ‘Adam’ and ‘The Blue Caftan.’ Beautiful things are reaching international audiences, the Cannes Film Festival and beyond. Long live cinema!“.

Industry observers note that she concluded the masterclass with a rallying cry for the moviegoing experience. “I hope cinema will never disappear because I truly believe in cinema as one of the cultural elements that are essential to humanity,” she noted.

Pizza chains are under pressure. GLP-1 use is only one part of the problem

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Big pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales.
  • Industry observers note that the pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza, Papa Johns, Little Caesars and Pizza Hut.
  • Recent findings suggest that these days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Big pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales.

Industry observers note that the pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza, Papa Johns, Little Caesars and Pizza Hut. But since dining rooms reopened, the biggest U.S. pizza chains have faced an uphill battle to retain their customers.

Recent findings suggest that these days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms. Plus, food quality and the customer experience have become more notable to diners who are looking for value when they order from restaurants.

Recent findings suggest that as a result of pizza fatigue and challenges facing the broader restaurant industry, the number of U.S. pizza restaurants has tumbled. Since pizza locations hit a peak of 83,035 nationwide in August 2019, more than 9,600 pizzerias had closed their doors as of July 2026, according to data from Datassential.

In a recent development, in 2025, sales at U.S. pizza restaurants fell 0.3%, according to Technomic data. Sales at independent pizzerias slipped 0.4%. Chains, which account for about two-thirds of the domestic pizza category sales, saw revenue shrink 0.3%.

Papa Johns reported that North American same-store sales declined 2.5% in 2025. Pizza Hut's U.S. same-store sales fell 5%. Among the three pizza chains that were publicly traded last year, only Domino's posted annual same-store sales growth at its U.S. restaurants, with an increase of 3%.

Sources indicate that it isn't just diners who have lost their appetite for pizza. Since March 2020, Papa Johns stock has lost about two-thirds of its value. Even shares of Domino's, which dominates the category, have seen gains of only about 2% in that time. For comparison, the S&P 500 has climbed about 150% over the same period.

And Yum Brands sold Pizza Hut this year, offloading the laggard of its portfolio to LongRange Capital and Yum China after about two decades of stagnating sales.

Recent findings suggest that "Pizza Hut has been a detractor for YUM ... Going forward, YUM won't be tripped up by pizza category dynamics (discounting, etc.), translating to stronger growth and higher concentration in higher growth industry segments and markets," Wells Fargo analyst Zachary Fadem wrote in a research note in September.

Pizza chains now have significantly more competition for diners' dollars than they did in 2020. Third-party delivery platforms, which grew in popularity during the pandemic, offer a wide variety of cuisines beyond the traditional pizza and Chinese. As a result, Domino's and Papa John's have to compete with other fast-food chains, like McDonald's and Chick-fil-A, for DoorDash and Uber Eats orders.

Recent findings suggest that as pizza has grown more expensive, a pie seems less appealing to budget-conscious diners. The average large cheese pizza is now almost $17, according to the 2026 Pizza Power Report from PMQ Pizza, a trade publication.

According to recent reports, plus, frozen pizza is another convenient option, with a lower price tag. Retail sales of single- and multi-serve frozen pizza rose 2.9% in the 52 weeks ended Nov. 7 compared with the same period in 2022, according to NielsenIQ data.

"When the American consumer is focused on the least expensive eating occasion, the items that are in my pantry, my refrigerator and my freezer win every single time," said David Portalatin, a food and food service industry advisor for Circana.

Convenience stores like Casey's General Stores have also won over customers with pizza at a low price point.

"We believe that [Casey's] has an advantage over [quick-service restaurants] and dollar stores, which have fewer options to navigate the persistent inflationary environment, while [Casey's] can offset food pressures with margins," Bank of America Securities analyst Sara Senatore wrote in a research note published in June.

She added that geographic overlap of locations suggests that Casey's is stealing share from Pizza Hut.

The biggest pizza chains have also been slow to adapt to shifting consumer attitudes toward nutrition. For example, of the four biggest chains, Papa Johns is the only one to even test a pizza crust with added protein as more diners prioritize it in their diets. And the test was only in one Atlanta restaurant — for a single day.

It has been revealed that pizza's nutritional content more broadly is another drag for the category. Its carbohydrate and fat content, from its dough and cheese, respectively, can make it less appealing for consumers on GLP-1 drugs, which have skyrocketed in use over the last several years.

Spending on pizza quick-service restaurants has fallen 22.2% per GLP-1 household after six to eight months using the medications, according to a 2026 survey published by PwC.

To be sure, pizza's recent struggles do not mean an existential crisis for the category. Total pizza servings are down only about 1% this year, Circana's Portalatin mentioned.

And chains are trying to reverse that downturn in servings. In August, Domino's rolled out the Domino, a customizable Detroit-style personal pizza to attract solo diners. In November, Papa Johns unveiled a latest turnaround strategy focusing on improving food consistency and restaurant operations. And Pizza Hut is running a holiday-themed meal deal.

"Pizza's not going anywhere," Portalatin stated. "The American consumer loves pizza.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, it’s not hyperbole: Netflix stock has been cut in half from its all-time high.
  • Black Friday streaming deals are an annual tradition at this point, but given the state of the business, they can also shed light on how the entertainment giants behind them are thinking about the future of their products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The streaming business is in flux, and Black Friday deals can help explain it.

According to recent reports, it’s not hyperbole: Netflix stock has been cut in half from its all-time high. Bundles are proliferating. And Skydance CEO David Ellison has made it clear that a merger of HBO Max and Paramount+ is a question of when, not if.

Black Friday streaming deals are an annual tradition at this point, but given the state of the business, they can also shed light on how the entertainment giants behind them are thinking about the future of their products.

HBO Max and Paramount+ are offering very different types of deals, even as their parent company Skydance, is actively preparing for a discount bundle set for early next year, and with a full merger of the services following later on.

HBO Max is offering an aggressive 50 percent discount on its ad-supported tier, charging $5.49 per month for a full year. Paramount+, meanwhile, is offering both its premium and standard plans for $2.99 per month, albeit only for the first two months.

With the bundle imminent and a merger coming (expect Paramount+’s tech stack to win out over HBO Max’s), the Black Friday deals are a last gasp before what is expected to be an aggressive discount campaign early next year.

The biggest new streamer to launch in the last year, Fox One, is offering a steep 75 percent discount, $5 for the first month, before it reverts back to $20 in month two.

Peacock, meanwhile, is offering generous discounts on both its select and premium aims, selling them for $2.99 and $8.99 per month for the first three months.

Disney, which has been leaning into bundles, is offering a year of Disney+ and Hulu for $5 per month, hoping to get viewers hooked on its two entertainment platforms (ESPN is the other) ahead of a full sunset of the Hulu standalone app (it is expected to continue as a standalone service within Disney+).

Apple TV, which is still trying to gain the scale that many of the other services already have, is offering an aggressive discount of over 50 percent, selling six months of the services for $6.99 per month, down from its typical price of $14.99 per month.

And niche streamers are being more aggressive: Look at Starz, which is offering an astonishing deal: $11.99 for 12 months, putting the price at under $1 per month when buying the annual strategy (a more modest discount is available on monthly plans), underscoring how it needs to gain scale, and fast. Crunchyroll, Sony’s anime-focused streamer, is also offering discounts of over 50 percent for six months, ranging from $3.99 for its base tier to $8.99 for its ultimate tier.

In a recent development, and it’s a world where Netflix, the king of the crop, still feels as though it has no need to offer discounts of any sort. After all, when you have won the subscription streaming war, it’s better to keep those margins intact.

#150739. A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1477 w)

A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside.
  • Researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them.
  • Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside. Scientists believe these mysterious objects, known as primordial black holes, could have formed during the first fraction of a second after the Major Bang, when extremely dense regions of matter collapsed under their own gravity. If they exist, these ancient remnants could also account for a substantial portion of dark matter, the invisible material that makes up most of the matter in the universe.

Researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them. Using theoretical calculations and computer simulations in three dimensions, the team investigated what would happen if a primordial black hole became trapped inside a star similar to our Sun.

Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility. A black hole no larger than an atom, but carrying the mass of an asteroid, could gradually sink toward the center of a star and begin consuming it from within.

Sources indicate that if the star rotates rapidly enough, material falling toward the black hole would eventually form a spinning disk around it. That development could set the stage for a catastrophic explosion.

"Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star," says lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

The interaction between the black hole and the surrounding disk could produce enormous jets of matter that punch through the star and cause it to explode within seconds. Researchers predict that the resulting outburst would emit intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays, potentially making it visible to telescopes already in operation.

"There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars," Gottlieb indicates. "We expect this to be visible, and it's something we should look into.".

The research team also included Matteo Cantiello of the Flatiron Institute, Cameron Norton and Matthew Kleban of New York University, and Ken Van Tilburg of Stanford University.

Ancient Black Holes That May Have Survived the Significant Bang.

According to recent reports, not every primordial black hole formed in the early universe would still exist today. According to a theory developed by physicist Stephen Hawking, black holes gradually lose energy through a quantum process called Hawking radiation. Over immense periods of time, this process causes them to shrink, and the smallest primordial black holes would already have evaporated completely.

Industry observers note that heavier primordial black holes, however, could have survived to the present day. Some might be approximately the size of an atom while containing as much mass as an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

Sources indicate that these extraordinary objects raise an intriguing question. If they are still scattered throughout the universe, what would happen when one encounters a star? More importantly, could the resulting interaction provide the evidence needed to establish that primordial black holes actually exist?

Recent findings suggest that to investigate, Gottlieb and his colleagues combined mathematical calculations with numerical simulations incorporating general relativity, fluid dynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics. Their goal was to understand how a primordial black hole could become trapped by a star and what would happen afterward.

How a Tiny Black Hole Could Become Trapped Inside a Star.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that a star acting alone generally could not capture a primordial black hole passing nearby. Its gravitational attraction would be insufficient to keep the black hole from escaping.

The situation changes when another object is involved. A companion star or planet could alter the gravitational interaction enough to allow the primordial black hole to become trapped.

In this arrangement involving three objects, the black hole could repeatedly travel through the star. Each passage would create friction as it moved through stellar material, gradually draining energy from its orbit and drawing it closer to the star's center.

The process could take thousands or even millions of years. Although that sounds extraordinarily slow, it is relatively brief compared with the age of the universe.

Eventually, the black hole would settle into the star's core, where it could begin feeding on the surrounding material.

"Then, this is where the action begins," Gottlieb notes.

A Black Hole Could Slowly Consume a Star From Within.

Once the primordial black hole reaches the stellar core, its growth depends partly on what happens to the energy generated as gas falls toward it. Some of that energy can heat the surrounding material, potentially slowing the rate at which additional gas falls inward.

According to recent reports, the team's simulations indicate that most of the energy would instead disappear into the black hole. This would allow it to accumulate matter more rapidly than earlier estimates suggested.

Sources indicate that over several million years, the growing black hole could consume approximately 1 percent of the star's total mass. At that stage, its fate would depend heavily on how quickly the star rotates.

Recent findings suggest that if the star spins fast enough, gas would no longer be able to plunge directly into the black hole. Instead, the material would gather into a rotating disk around the black hole, which would by then have grown to several meters in size.

In a recent development, "Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk," Gottlieb says. "The black hole is also spinning, and it's twisting space and time.".

As the disk continues feeding the black hole, the extreme rotation twists the magnetic field threading the surrounding material. This process could generate exceptionally powerful jets that shoot outward from the black hole's poles.

"This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole," Gottlieb explains. "And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It's very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.".

What began as a tiny black hole hidden inside an otherwise ordinary star could therefore end in a violent explosion, with the star's destruction unfolding in a matter of seconds once the critical conditions are reached.

Exploding Stars Could Reveal Primordial Black Holes and Dark Matter.

The researchers also calculated what these unusual explosions might look like to astronomers, estimating how their brightness and color would change across different wavelengths of light.

Industry observers note that their models predict a recognizable sequence of emissions, beginning with high-energy radiation and progressing through other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum as the explosion evolves. The initial outburst could include intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with gamma rays and X-rays.

Recent findings suggest that "We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions," Gottlieb indicates. "This is something we could potentially detect, if it's not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.".

Such signals could be detectable with existing astronomical instruments, potentially allowing researchers to search for primordial black holes far beyond the Milky Way.

However, identifying one would not be straightforward. Other cosmic events can generate similar flashes of radiation, so an unusual explosion alone would not establish that a primordial black hole was responsible.

Astronomers would need to examine additional evidence, including the characteristics of the exploding star. One especially revealing clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not ordinarily be expected to meet such a violent end.

It has been revealed that "For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside," Gottlieb says. "The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.".

Even if no convincing examples are found, the search could help scientists determine how common primordial black holes might be and how much dark matter they could account for.

In a recent development, for now, primordial black holes remain hypothetical. But the new research offers astronomers a possible observational signature to pursue, connecting the spectacular destruction of stars with objects that may have existed since the universe's earliest moments.

It has been revealed that the research received partial support from the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program and the National Science Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman on charges of spying for Russia started Thursday.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court stated.

Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses. Her lawyers caused further delay when they said she would not confirm her personal information.

Sources indicate that several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys remarked their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.

The Russian ambassador was summoned regarding the incident, and Andrei Mayerov, the deputy military attache at the embassy, was expelled from Germany.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.

It has been revealed that her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws. She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.

She was also remarked to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

Sources indicate that on several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Berlin summoned the alleged handler, who was identified by Der Spiegel magazine as the embassy's deputy military attache, over the incident and expelled him from Germany.

Industry observers note that ilona W. led an advocacy group for years that called for international cooperation, focusing particularly on German, Russian, Ukrainian relations.

In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.

Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within the military.

The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.

He also said "he may have seen her himself at an event.".

Sources indicate that "But she is not a Russian citizen and, as far as we are aware, has no ties to Russia. She is a German and Ukrainian citizen, and, frankly, we do not associate with such individuals here," he said.

Scam Roblox cheat codes are injecting malware into computers, reports reveal

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kids looking for an easy edge in Roblox may be giving scammers access to the whole family computer.
  • Industry observers note that A Cybernews investigation found that Roblox generated more than 22 million cheat-related searches from 2018 to 2026.
  • It has been revealed that with some context, it's understandable why Roblox makes for an easy target.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kids looking for an easy edge in Roblox may be giving scammers access to the whole family computer.

Industry observers note that A Cybernews investigation found that Roblox generated more than 22 million cheat-related searches from 2018 to 2026. That's more than half of all the cheat searches across the 17 major games the outlet tracked. Security researchers working at Cybernews say scammers are using that demand to pass off malware as working cheats.

It has been revealed that with some context, it's understandable why Roblox makes for an easy target. The platform is free to download, but many of the games inside it put weapons, VIP perks, and rare items behind paywalls. Those usually cost between $5 and $50, according to Cybernews. That has led to a steady stream of stories about kids running up charges on a parent's credit card, and the RobloxHelp subreddit is full of parents asking how to get their money back.

"Kids without access to credit cards look to cut corners on YouTube and Google search," Cybernews writes in its report.

No other game in Cybernews' study came close. Over the past 12 months, Roblox drew nearly 3.9 million cheat searches. Counter-Strike 2 came in second with about 533,000. Adjusted for player count, Roblox gets 482 cheat searches per 1,000 players, more than six times Minecraft's rate.

It has been revealed that many Roblox cheats rely on script executors — third-party programs that let players run their own code inside Roblox games. Antivirus software routinely flags these tools, so young players have gotten used to clicking past Windows Defender warnings, according to Cybernews. Many also hand full administrator access to unverified files they found through YouTube videos and Discord servers. Recent findings suggest that back in March, a threat actor listed 50 million allegedly stolen Roblox logins for sale. Cybernews states they were likely collected by password-stealing malware running on infected devices.

A few months later, in August, security firm Bitdefender uncovered a campaign spreading fake "undetected" versions of Xeno, a popular Roblox executor, Cybernews reported. The downloads came with real cheat scripts so they'd appear to work, but also contained malware. That malware could steal Roblox logins, saved browser passwords, and Discord accounts. It could also record keystrokes and even capture webcam footage.

These kinds of scams are even riskier if Roblox is played on a shared computer. If a child uses the same computer their parents use, malware can steal a parent's saved banking logins, work email, and personal files, too.

Last year, Check Point Research found a similar scheme aimed at Minecraft players. Fake mods posing as the popular cheat tools Oringo and Taunahi were spread through malicious GitHub repositories. They infected more than 1,500 devices starting in March 2025, TechSpot reported. The malware went after browser passwords, crypto wallets, and Steam accounts.

Industry observers note that part of why these schemes work is that growing up online isn't the same as knowing how a computer works. Younger generations grew up on phones and apps that hide things like file permissions and security settings, so a warning on a desktop computer can be easy to dismiss. A 2023 Dell Technologies survey of more than 15,000 people ages 18 to 26 found that 44 percent were taught only very basic digital skills in school, and 12 percent got no digital skills education at all, according to Fortune.

#150735. Mysterious upcoming viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1085 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Mysterious upcoming viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history.
  • Industry observers note that the research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins.
  • Industry observers note that the discovery could have notable implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and tiny protein compartments inside cells, offering fresh clues about how some of life's earliest biological structures may have developed.

Industry observers note that the research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins. Scientists previously believed these compartments evolved from viruses. However, the latest evidence suggests a more complicated evolutionary relationship in which viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

Industry observers note that the discovery could have notable implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life. It also raises the possibility that viruses have biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.

Mysterious Upcoming Viruses Reveal an Evolutionary Connection.

At the center of the discovery are proteins that fold into a distinctive three-dimensional structure known as the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are found in both viruses and encapsulins.

In a recent development, the newly identified viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. They also possess characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, making them possible evolutionary intermediates between the two. Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared.

"What makes the HK97-fold proteins so interesting is that they can form shells that enclose biochemical reactions in cellular lineages, archaea, and bacteria. But they also serve genetic purposes in viruses, storing and protecting their viral genome," mentioned Abelardo Aguilar, the study's first author and a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami College of Arts and Sciences.

"These proteins build compartments with two different roles, which connects directly with the study of the origin of life and its early evolution because if you think about it, life at its core is about enclosing reactions and also enclosing information that can be inherited so those reactions can happen in the future.".

AI Helps Discover Hidden Viruses in Billions of DNA Sequences.

In a recent development, to uncover these previously unknown viruses, Aguilar worked with Antoni Luque Santolaria, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Biology. Luque also holds secondary appointments in the Department of Physics within the College of Arts and Sciences and the Department of Chemical, Environmental and Materials Engineering in the College of Engineering. The project brought together collaborators from multiple institutions.

In a recent development, rather than relying on laboratory experiments to grow viruses, the team searched enormous genetic databases containing billions of DNA sequences. They combined bioinformatics, models of protein behavior, and artificial intelligence tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, to investigate the structures encoded by these sequences.

Sources indicate that the databases included IMG/M, a resource associated with the U.S. Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute and the University of California, Berkeley. Its genetic information comes from environmental samples collected around the world, including soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut, and numerous other locations.

This approach allows scientists to investigate viruses that have never been successfully grown in a laboratory, greatly expanding the number of organisms and evolutionary relationships they can study.

According to recent reports, "The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab. But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don't know the host, that we can't culture in the lab, but that are everywhere," Luque explained. "That means there are multiple questions in relation to evolution and how viruses have adapted to the world that it's now possible to explore bioinformatically.".

Viral Protein Shells May Have Unexpected Functions.

Beyond identifying the newly introduced viruses, the researchers proposed a possible molecular explanation for how viruses and encapsulins could have evolved from one another.

In a recent development, their model centers on procapsids, immature viral protein shells (capsids) that may provide a pathway between the two types of structures. These shells could potentially support both genetic functions, such as containing viral DNA, and metabolic functions involving chemical reactions.

This raises an intriguing possibility. Viral capsids are generally recognized for packaging and protecting genetic material, but certain forms might also help create environments where biochemical reactions can occur.

"One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole," Aguilar explained.

Although further research is needed to establish these potential functions, the findings suggest that scientists may need to look beyond the infectious stages of viruses to fully understand their roles in nature.

"When we're looking at viruses, we tend to look only at the particles that are infective, and this study points out that we might need to start putting more emphasis on the non-infective versions of the virus and what other functions those viral-like particles may have that we have overlooked in the past.".

Newly introduced AI Tools Open the Door to More Viral Discoveries.

In a recent development, the research also demonstrates how artificial intelligence and computational biology are transforming the study of viruses. By combining powerful analytical tools with knowledge of protein structure and physical behavior, scientists can now investigate evolutionary questions that were previously difficult to explore.

Sources indicate that supported by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and the U.S. National Science Foundation, the project provides a framework for studying other poorly understood viruses and their biological capabilities.

The researchers believe these methods could also be useful beyond evolutionary biology, including efforts to understand newly emerging viruses and pathogens.

"If you have the right question and you pair it with the right tools and physical insights, it gives researchers an opportunity to look at viruses in a way that we didn't have an opportunity to do before," Luque stated. "There are evolution questions, but there are also questions about emerging pathogens or emerging viruses. The set of tools that we use can be moved forward in different contexts.".

Materials provided by University of Miami. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Marvel veteran Sebastian Stan is sticking up for last year’s “Thunderbolts,” despite it being one of the lowest-grossing MCU movies.

According to recent reports, in the team-up movie, he reprised his role as Bucky Barnes, aka the Winter Soldier, alongside Florence Pugh as Yelena Belova and David Harbour as the Red Guardian to form the Thunderbolts, a latest group in the MCU. They later renamed themselves the New Avengers, made up of Wyatt Russell as U.S. Agent, Lewis Pullman as Sentry and Hannah John-Kamen as Ghost, and the team will return in next month’s “Avengers: Doomsday.” Related Stories John Travolta Didn’t Recognize Himself as Alleged JFK Assassin Johnny Roselli in ‘November 1963’: ‘I Went, "Oh My God, He’s the Devil"’ Gérard Depardieu to Stand Trial for Rape Charges After Failed Appeal.

After releasing in May 2025, “Thunderbolts” ended its box office run with $382 million worldwide, ranking as the fifth lowest total out of all 38 MCU films. The only movies below it are “Black Widow” ($379 million), “Captain America: The First Avenger” ($370 million), “The Incredible Hulk” ($264 million) and “The Marvels” ($206 million). They’re all a far cry from this summer’s “Spider-Man: Brand Newly introduced Day,” which is the second biggest MCU movie with $2.5 billion (behind the highest-grossing film ever, “Avengers: Endgame” with $2.94 billion).

“I think it’s just when you’ve had a studio and you’ve had Marvel and it’s been so many years where they’ve just been knocking it out of the park, $350 million global, something like that, it just suddenly doesn’t seem that much,” Stan said on “Next Best Picture.” “But it’s insane how much money that is.”.

He added, “For us, it felt like a success. I know a lot of care went into that and it had more nuance to it in terms of some of the recent ones, from my point of view at least, dealing with real issues like mental health and depression and so on.”.

Industry observers note that “Thunderbolts” was praised by fans and critics for its darker tone and how it elevated its cast of misfit, lesser-known characters. Its director, Jake Schreier, was tapped by Marvel to helm its 2028 “X-Men” movie, with a cast including Sadie Sink, Adam Driver, Inde Navarrette, Kit Connor and more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Merritt R. Turetsky Profile (2026).

Boglands are formed by waterlogged conditions and a lack of oxygen that slows down plant decomposition, causing organic matter to accumulate as a thick layer of peat. Peatlands occupy only 3% of the planet’s land area, but store about 30% of soil carbon. “In this liminal space, where land is water and water is land,” writes ecologist Merritt Turetsky, “a strange and haunting loveliness reveals itself.” This is not obvious to most people, who often laugh when told that she studies bogs. Such sceptics will be won over by her fascinating book.

Leah C. Stokes MIT Press (2026).

At university, environmentalist Leah Stokes was stirred by the 2006 documentary An Inconvenient Truth, which argued that each of us is responsible for reducing global warming. Only later, as an associate professor in California, did she realize that the chief culprit is fossil-fuel infrastructure. In 2022, Stokes had a major role in pushing the US government to pass landmark legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act, with more than US$400 billion in climate investments. Her absorbing book unpacks “the blow-by-blows of how this climate law was made”.

James K. Galbraith Univ. Chicago Press (2026).

Recent findings suggest that veteran economist James Galbraith begins his striking attack on mainstream economics in the United States by declaring that his academic discipline has long been a “fraud”. For decades, economists have embraced the idea that “power over money should be kept far from democratic politics”. And yet, oligarchs from finance, technology, pharmaceuticals and several other fields now hold political power. Economists, he argues, continue to deploy outdated tools from a century ago, which are weakening democracy.
