German Catholic Church abuse victims may receive higher compensation

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled on Thursday that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay €550,000 ($603,341) to a now 60-year-old woman.
  • This ruling could result in the Catholic Church paying significantly higher compensation to victims of abuse and sexual violence by priests.
  • The settlement far exceeds previous sums granted in similar cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled on Thursday that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay €550,000 ($603,341) to a now 60-year-old woman. Melanie F.*, the claimant, was subjected to serious sexual abuse by a priest in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

This ruling could result in the Catholic Church paying significantly higher compensation to victims of abuse and sexual violence by priests.

The settlement far exceeds previous sums granted in similar cases. Before this, the highest financial compensation awarded by a court was €300,000. This amount was granted by the Regional Court of Cologne in June 2023 to a former altar boy who was abused by a priest for several years.

Sources indicate that melanie F. was represented by the same lawyer. Since she had already received €360,000 in compensation during previous proceedings, the court granted Melanie F. an additional €190,000.

In determining the appropriate amount of damages, the Seventh Civil Senate of the Higher Regional Court of Cologne pointed to an "abortion performed without the knowledge or consent of the plaintiff, who was only 15 years old at the time" as one of the deciding factors. The judges mentioned that this incident in particular warranted a substantial increase in compensatory damages. The teenager reportedly became pregnant twice during the period of abuse.

Born in 1966, Melanie F. lived in a Catholic orphanage in Bonn in the late 1970s. Bernd U., then a theology student, worked there as a volunteer and cared for several children. After he was ordained as a priest, he took Melanie and a boy two years her senior from the orphanage to live with him.

Industry observers note that beginning in 1979, he subjected the underage Melanie to severe sexual abuse in his residence at the parish. He threatened to send her back to the orphanage if she refused to comply. He subsequently became the legal guardian of both children. Cardinal Joseph Höffner, who was then the Archbishop of Cologne, approved the arrangement.

In its written opinion, the court addressed the question of whether an archdiocese can be held liable for the criminal acts of a member of the clergy. The judges decided to overrule the Cologne Regional Court's ruling from 2023 and gave a detailed explanation of their reasoning. Ultimately, they found that the Church was liable under the principles of official liability.

Industry observers note that the Regional Court had previously rejected this argument in 2023, siding with the lawyers of the Archdiocese of Cologne. At the time, the judges ruled that the abuse was not sufficiently linked to Bernd U.'s role as a priest. According to the judges, he had abused his foster child in his capacity as a caregiver, not as part of his priestly duties.

The 2023 ruling was met with disbelief and anger within the Archdiocese of Cologne. The archdiocese was already in turmoil because many Catholics were unhappy with how Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki handled abuse cases. For decades, Church teachings and statements by Cologne's archbishops had repeatedly emphasized that a priest is a priest in all that he does and cannot simply set that role aside.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But now, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne has concluded that there is in fact a clear connection between Bernd U.'s work for the church and the crimes he committed.

Industry observers note that in their decision, they explained that he had assumed a pastoral role in caring for Melanie F. while she was still living in the orphanage and gained her trust through displays of great affection.

His role at the church was described explicitly by the judges as a "cover." It was only much later that he sought to become the children's foster father, a position he would likely not have been able to obtain so easily without the "cover" of being a celibate Catholic priest. In addition, most of the abuse took place in the rectory.

After the ruling, Melanie F. said she was relieved that her years-long legal battle had finally come to an end. But she said she would never be able to put the abuse behind her. "You can't just block it out; you live with it.".

The Archdiocese of Cologne stated it "respectfully" took note of the decision.

Sources indicate that the perpetrator, now 74 years old, was sentenced to 12 years in prison at his 2022 trial. The court found that he had abused nine girls, the youngest of whom was nine years old. The Church subsequently removed him from the priesthood.

Recent findings suggest that "The strategy of the Archdiocese of Cologne to portray its priests' serious sexual crimes as the actions of private individuals has failed miserably," Thomas Schüller, a Catholic canon lawyer, told DW. Schüller described the archdiocese's approach as a "cynical attempt" that betrays the Catholic Church's own understanding of the priestly office.

From now on, the church will be held liable if a priest uses his position to sexually abuse children or teenagers and if the diocese or Protestant regional church has failed to fulfill its supervisory duties adequately.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Schüller said that Germany's Catholic bishops must "significantly increase" compensation payments to survivors. Until now, the bishops had consistently argued that the amounts should be based on current court rulings and legal standards.

However, this ruling will now have "significant financial consequences for both churches," he noted, describing the ruling as "a day of hope for many survivors of sexual abuse in both churches.".

Matthias Katsch, spokesperson for the survivor advocacy group Eckiger Tisch, also called the ruling "good news.".

It has been revealed that "Today, it was made clear that the Church must pay for the harm caused by its officials," he said. However, he added that the amount was still too low given the horrific nature of the crimes and their lifelong consequences.

It has been revealed that "The Archdiocese of Cologne's leadership turned a blind eye or acted with the grossest negligence," he remarked, allowing the crimes to happen. Melanie F. had sought compensation of between €800,000 and €900,000.

Sources indicate that in March 2026, the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments (UKA), which was established by the German Bishops' Conference in 2021, announced that it had approved payments totaling approximately €93 million for survivors in all dioceses. Since then, several dioceses have published additional studies containing new reports of abuse cases.

Sixteen years after survivors and Jesuit priest Klaus Mertes helped bring the abuse scandal to light, the German Bishops' Conference will now have to prepare for significantly higher compensation payments.

In the United States, where civil lawsuits seeking compensation often involve far higher sums than in Germany, a number of Catholic dioceses have filed for bankruptcy. But that is unlikely to happen in Germany. The Bonn-based law firm of Eberhard Luetjohann, Melanie F.'s attorney, has reported receiving inquiries from hundreds of abuse survivors seeking higher compensation.

Spokesperson for Eckiger Tisch, Matthias Katsch, called on church leaders to engage in dialogue with survivors and their advocacy groups. Katsch said the question of the Church's liability for crimes committed by priests lies at the heart of most cases in which survivors are dissatisfied with the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments' decisions and believe they are entitled to higher compensation.

It is unacceptable, he noted, that these survivors must go to court to obtain the compensation they deserve.

This article was originally written in German.

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

#150715. This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1074 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a massive impression on scientists.
  • It has been revealed that the species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes.
  • Industry observers note that many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a massive impression on scientists. Although it is only about the size of a quarter, the spider has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome.

It has been revealed that the species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes. Its unusually large genome seems particularly fitting given Colbert's famously pompous television persona on the former Comedy Central show "The Colbert Report.".

Industry observers note that many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween. But this particular spider stands out for something that cannot be seen with the naked eye: the extraordinary amount of DNA packed into its tiny body.

"At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it's not the largest genome among the spiders, but it's significant," remarked corresponding author Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology.

Recent findings suggest that according to Bond, this is the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a spider belonging to this family. The findings were published in the Journal of Heredity.

A Secretive Spider That Hunts From Underground.

In a recent development, visitors to the coastal dunes of Northern California may unknowingly pass close to these spiders without ever spotting one. Most of their lives unfold beneath the sand, where they remain hidden in carefully constructed burrows.

Sources indicate that female trapdoor spiders spend their entire lives underground in tunnels lined with silk. Each burrow has a hinged entrance that blends into its surroundings, allowing the spider to stay concealed while monitoring activity outside.

It has been revealed that when an unsuspecting insect or other prey animal approaches, vibrations alert the spider to its presence. At precisely the right moment, the spider bursts through its hidden door to capture its next meal.

Although these spiders are skilled ambush predators, their venom poses no danger to humans. Bond noted that among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.

A Spider Genome Bigger Than the Human Genome.

The spider's DNA contains more surprises than its sheer size. Researchers found that its genome includes 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human cells, which are organized into 23 pairs.

According to recent reports, however, having a larger genome does not necessarily mean having more genes. In this spider, approximately 77% of the genome consists of repetitive DNA sequences that appear many times throughout its genetic material.

The research also highlights an unusual feature of spider chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional repetitive DNA sequences associated with telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. This difference could help explain why spider chromosomes appear to evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.

"It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life," Bond said.

Why Is the Spider Named After Stephen Colbert?

The story behind the spider's unusual scientific name dates back to 2008, when Stephen Colbert discovered that Bond had named a trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young.

Recent findings suggest that not wanting to be left out, Colbert turned the situation into a comedy segment. During "Who's Not Honoring Me Now?" on "The Colbert Report," he publicly demanded that Bond name a spider in his honor.

Bond agreed, and Aptostichus stephencolberti became Colbert's namesake in the spider world.

Rising Seas Threaten California's Trapdoor Spiders.

Beyond revealing the spider's genetic peculiarities, the research could play an crucial role in protecting the species.

The genome sequencing effort is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative designed to build a collection of genomic information that scientists can use to guide conservation decisions.

Trapdoor spiders generally do not venture far from their burrows, making it difficult for populations to move between habitats. Because their coastal dune environments are already separated into isolated areas, researchers hope genetic information will help them identify distinct populations that may need special protection.

According to recent reports, "We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us," Bond said. "We're hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.".

Aptostichus stephencolberti (the "t" in Colbert is silent) is found only in coastal dunes along a limited stretch of Central California, extending from the San Francisco Bay area to Monterey.

This restricted range makes the species particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels could eliminate portions of its coastal habitat, while invasive species pose another significant danger.

"They're going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they're also very sensitive to invasive species," Bond stated.

Spider Venom Could Hold Clues to Latest Medicines.

Sources indicate that the potential benefits of studying this spider's genome extend beyond conservation and evolutionary biology. Scientists also hope that understanding spider genetics will help them explore the vast range of chemical compounds found in spider venom.

Some substances identified in spider venoms have shown promise as potential painkillers, while others could be useful in developing upcoming ways to control agricultural pests.

With so many spider species still poorly understood at the genetic level, researchers believe their venoms may contain valuable compounds that have yet to be discovered.

"We don't really know what's out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms," Bond said.

The study's additional authors include Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe and Oanh Nguyen of UC Davis; Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann and Merly Escalona of UC Santa Cruz; Robert D. Cooper of Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University; and H. Bradley Shaffer and Erin Toffelmier of UCLA.

The research received support from the California Conservation Genomics Project, with funding provided to the University of California through the state of California's State Budget Act of 2019, as well as from the National Science Foundation.

Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.
  • The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.
  • Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.

The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.

Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.

According to recent reports, "I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.

He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.

Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.

A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.

Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly Germany's renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), are reluctant to recruit from places like India, say observers.

"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively fresh concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," noted Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.

The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja mentioned.

This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Saikia, the butcher, had studied German to the B1 level, considered intermediate proficiency. He soon realized it was not enough for everyday communication at work.

It has been revealed that "Initially, I found the theory classes of my Ausbildung quite difficult. But my co-workers helped me. After one year, my German improved, and I realized integration happened automatically as my language level improved," he remarked.

David Kipp, researcher in the Global Issues Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), stated he's "skeptical" about lowering language requirements.

Sources indicate that "Language skills are an notable selection criterion so people actually know where they are going. Sending people with very little language knowledge makes exploitation easier, because they have less direct contact with German institutions," he told DW.

Language, however, isn't the only hurdle.

Raja said workers' councils also often resist hiring from abroad.

It has been revealed that "Tech giant decisions in the Mittelstand involve the team and the shop floor," he pointed out. "In some cases, the workers' council resists hiring from India because they mistakenly believe 'cheap Indian labor' will take their jobs or undercut their wages.".

Raja mentioned he often uses unconventional outreach methods, including hosting TikTok Live sessions, to engage directly with industrial employers and workers and dispel concerns and misconceptions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

German companies have traditionally relied on workers from Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations such as Poland, Romania and Slovenia to fill labor market gaps.

But studies show CEE workers are increasingly reluctant to relocate to Germany, as faster economic growth and stronger career prospects improve opportunities in their home countries.

The situation has prompted recruitment agencies in these countries to look beyond the European Union for workers.

Sources indicate that these third-country nationals (TCNs) obtain residence permits in CEE states and are then posted to German job sites under the Vander Elst visa. The mechanism allows non-EU citizens legally employed in one EU member state to be temporarily sent to work in another.

"European Labour Authority's (ELA) 2025 study on the posting of third-country nationals found that the number of posted TCNs is increasing. The main sectors concerned are construction and transport," remarked Pia Fallstrom, ELA spokesperson.

The exact number of TCNs posted across the EU is difficult to gauge, as data exchange between sending and receiving countries by nationality and sector is limited.

"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.

While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.

"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.

"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Raja noted he had seen cases of workers falling victim to recruitment scams and being exploited as a result.

Recent findings suggest that "I know of a family that took out a loan so that their child could enroll in an institute which promised a job in Germany," said Raja. "When the candidate realized it's a scam, they ended up in Bahrain doing a tough manual labor job just to pay off the loan.".

Saikia, the butcher, stressed the importance of workers verifying that a recruitment agency is legitimate.

In his case, he noted the agency's detailed website and its CEO's willingness to speak with him during the early stages of the recruitment process gave him confidence that it was not a scam.

Kipp, the SWP expert, argued that preventing exploitative hiring practices requires streamlining migration procedures, expanding pre-departure cultural training and becoming more effective at identifying trusted entities and combating social media scams.

Industry observers note that "India is the most important country for experimenting with how work migration functions. If we don't pay attention, we'll just send people into the low-wage sector and into disappointment," he said.

#150711. Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (809 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
  • Industry observers note that researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown.
  • Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. For approximately one hour, the star gradually grew brighter before fading back to its usual appearance. The change was smooth and symmetrical, with no sudden explosion or flare. It looked as though an invisible object had moved between Earth and the star, bending its light in our direction. Afterward, the star returned to normal and showed no further changes in brightness.

Industry observers note that researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown. The event appears to be an example of gravitational microlensing, a phenomenon predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. When a compact object with sufficient mass passes in front of a distant star, its gravity bends the star's light and temporarily magnifies its brightness. This produces a recognizable pattern that differs from the changes caused by variable stars, stellar flares, or passing asteroids.

Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The distinctive pattern convinced the team that they had detected a genuine gravitational microlensing event. What remained uncertain was the nature of the invisible object responsible.

Three Possible Explanations for the Mysterious Object.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have identified three potential explanations for Phoebe. One possibility is a rogue planet that was expelled from its original solar system and now travels alone through the Milky Way. Another is a similar wandering planet located within the Large Magellanic Cloud. If the second explanation proves correct, Phoebe would become the first planet discovered through gravitational microlensing beyond our galaxy.

The third possibility is far more extraordinary. Phoebe could be a primordial black hole, an ancient object that formed in the earliest moments of the universe. Unlike ordinary black holes, which develop when massive stars collapse, primordial black holes could have emerged from extremely dense regions of space during the first fractions of a second after the Major Bang. Such objects would have formed long before the first stars appeared.

A One-Hour Signal Reveals a Surprising Clue.

Industry observers note that the unusually short duration of the brightening provides an important clue about Phoebe's mass. Gravitational microlensing events depend partly on how massive the intervening object is. Generally, lighter objects produce shorter events, although their speed and position also influence how long the magnification lasts.

Phoebe's signal lasted approximately 60 minutes, placing it near the detection limit of current astronomical surveys. Using the observed duration and their models of the event, researchers estimated that the object has a mass roughly three times that of the Moon. That would make it considerably less massive than any planet in our solar system and far too small to be a conventional black hole formed by a collapsing star.

Black holes produced through stellar collapse typically have masses of at least about five times that of the Sun. Phoebe's estimated mass falls enormously below that threshold. If the mysterious object really is a black hole, its tiny mass would point toward a primordial origin rather than the death of a star.

Could Phoebe Be a Primordial Black Hole Linked to Dark Matter?

In a recent development, to investigate where Phoebe might belong, the researchers compared the likelihood that the object originated from different populations. These included stars in the Milky Way, stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and objects associated with the surrounding dark matter halo.

In a recent development, the results strongly favored the dark matter halo. According to the team's calculations, Phoebe is approximately 100,000 times more likely to belong to this population than to one associated with ordinary stellar matter. This enormous difference makes a potential connection to dark matter particularly intriguing, although it does not establish that Phoebe is a primordial black hole.

If the primordial black hole interpretation is correct, Phoebe could be among the oldest objects ever detected. It may have formed before the first atoms and stars existed, when the universe was still experiencing the extreme conditions that followed the Major Bang.

For roughly 13 billion years, such an object could have traveled unseen through space, leaving almost no trace of its existence. Then, on a single night in December 2019, its gravity may have briefly magnified the light of a distant star, offering astronomers a remarkable glimpse of something born near the very beginning of the universe.

It has been revealed that the Richat Structure, also known as the “Eye of the Sahara,” is seen from the International Space Station as it orbited above on Nov. 14, 2026. It is an eroded geological dome about 100 million years old created by igneous activity and uplift in the nation of Mauritania. In this type of geologic structure, rocks exposed in the center of the “bullseye” are older than rocks forming the outer rings. This structure measures 45 kilometers (28 miles) across and is made up of igneous and sedimentary rocks.

#150707. Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard

Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood.
  • Sources indicate that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled.
  • Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

Sources indicate that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”.

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

In a recent development, “I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”.

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

Recent findings suggest that she began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.

When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

Sources indicate that “Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she said, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”.

As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test prepares, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

“While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” mentioned Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”.

The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

“Ashley is a great team player. This conversion is a fantastic milestone because it unlocks new avenues for her learning and development, and allows us to integrate her into new roles,” stated Linnette Morales, Knight’s supervisor in the Program Analysis Office. “I am thrilled she can now fully access the opportunities on the civil servant side, immensely benefiting both her continued career growth and our organization.”.

Recent findings suggest that the workforce directive, entitled “Restoring NASA’s Core Competencies” and announced by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in February, is part of a broader effort to expand the agency’s critical institutional knowledge, increase resources essential for mission success, and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.

Recent findings suggest that “The directive has given our office an opportunity to rebalance positions across the organization and remove limitations that were applied to those who were previously not government employees,” noted Lisa Kelleher, Goddard’s chief financial officer. “We are now better able to insource many of our experienced contractor staff, allowing us to build up our in-house core competencies in areas such as budget analysis and accounting, and in turn increase our support for mission success.”.

For Knight, she sees an increasing importance for her organization and hopes to make impactful contributions, especially as work taking place at Goddard helps NASA return a crewed mission to the lunar surface, build a Moon Base, and eventually send humans to Mars.

“We’re the go-between between NASA Headquarters and Goddard programs, and it’s our job to make it a seamless transition for projects to use money they’ve been given to help get these projects off the ground,” she remarked. “It’s both vital and exciting with the lunar and Mars endeavors, and I’m proud to play whatever role I can.”.

Decades after first following her parents around center, and now following in their footsteps as a NASA civil servant, Knight is as captivated by Goddard and its people as she was during her early visits.

“Through the years, I’ve noticed everyone remains driven by teamwork and achieving the mission,” she mentioned. “Everybody wants to succeed together by working toward the same goal, and I’m grateful I can continue to be part of it all.”.

#150706. Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1408 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans.
  • Sources indicate that A new study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer.
  • The discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans. Yet scientists are still working to answer a fundamental question about our planet's history: Where did all this carbon originally come from?

Sources indicate that A new study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer. Researchers have uncovered chemical evidence suggesting that much of Earth's carbon may have arrived aboard ancient meteorites during a particular stage of the planet's formation. Even more remarkably, the findings suggest that some of this carbon became trapped deep inside Earth's core before eventually making its way back to the surface.

The discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks. Researchers believe these chemical fingerprints may reveal carbon that originated in Earth's core and traveled upward through the planet's interior.

"We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth's core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface," indicates lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor in Columbia University's Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How Carbon Could Escape From Earth's Core.

To understand how carbon might travel from Earth's deepest interior to its surface, it helps to look at the planet's internal structure.

Beneath Earth's thin outer crust lies the mantle, a vast region of mostly solid rock extending approximately 1,800 miles downward. Below that is the outer core, a roughly 1,400-mile-thick layer of molten metal surrounding the extremely hot, dense, solid metallic inner core.

According to recent reports, scientists believe that most of Earth's carbon is stored in its core. However, directly examining this material is far beyond the reach of current technology, and researchers may never be able to obtain samples from such extreme depths.

Fortunately, Earth's volcanic activity offers another way to investigate what lies below.

Sources indicate that recent studies suggest that certain elements can escape from the outer core and enter the overlying mantle. From there, they may be transported toward the surface by enormous rising columns of hot rock known as mantle plumes.

These plumes begin near the boundary between the core and mantle. As they ascend, some of the rock partially melts, producing magma that can eventually erupt through volcanoes.

It has been revealed that when that magma cools, crystals begin to grow. Occasionally, these crystals trap tiny droplets of molten material before dissolved gases have a chance to escape. The trapped droplets, known as undegassed melt inclusions, preserve valuable chemical information about the original magma.

"These melts are fossils of the magma," Moussallam says.

Because magma contains dissolved gases, including carbon dioxide, these microscopic pockets provide scientists with a rare opportunity to study carbon that may have traveled upward from Earth's core.

Hawaiian Volcanoes Reveal an Unusual Carbon Signature.

Hawaii is particularly well suited for this kind of investigation. Previous research has established that its volcanoes receive magma associated with a deep mantle plume, potentially providing access to material originating near the boundary with Earth's core.

Recent findings suggest that moussallam and his colleagues examined volcanic rocks from eruptions at Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift. Using a recently developed analytical technique, they measured carbon isotopes preserved inside undegassed melt inclusions.

Carbon isotopes are different forms of the same element that have slightly different masses. By comparing their relative abundance, scientists can identify chemical signatures that offer clues about where carbon came from and what processes it experienced.

The Tantalus Rift samples are thought to represent magma originating near the outer margins of the mantle plume. Earlier research established that typical mantle carbon has an isotopic signature between approximately -5 and -7 per mil, a measurement expressing small differences in isotope ratios. The researchers found that the Tantalus Rift samples closely matched this expected range.

The Kīlauea samples, however, told a very different story.

Recent findings suggest that magma beneath Kīlauea is believed to originate closer to the center of the mantle plume, where material may rise from near the core-mantle boundary. In these samples, the scientists detected carbon with a much heavier isotopic signature of approximately -1 per mil.

This unusual value has rarely been observed before and differs substantially from the signature normally associated with Earth's mantle.

"This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle," says Moussallam. "This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core.".

Although the team considers Earth's core the most likely source, Moussallam emphasizes that the evidence is not yet definitive. Additional measurements will be necessary to establish whether the carbon truly originated there.

Ancient Meteorites May Explain Where Earth's Carbon Came From.

The unusual carbon signature also provided researchers with a possible clue about events that occurred more than 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was still forming.

According to Moussallam, the isotopic composition of carbon in Earth's core should preserve "the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created.".

To investigate that possibility, the team compared the distinctive Kīlauea measurements with carbon signatures found in ancient meteorites. They discovered similarities to a group of meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites.

Sources indicate that chondrites are among the oldest known materials in our solar system, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. They preserve clues about the primitive material from which planets formed.

"All of Earth is made of chondrites," Moussallam explains. "They're the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets.".

Scientists generally distinguish between two broad categories of chondrites. Noncarbonaceous chondrites formed in the inner solar system, while carbonaceous chondrites, which contain more carbon, originated in the outer regions of the solar system.

Exactly how much each type contributed to Earth's formation has remained a subject of scientific debate.

The new findings support the possibility that carbonaceous chondrites made an especially notable contribution during the later stages of Earth's development.

Recent findings suggest that according to the researchers' proposed explanation, these carbon-rich meteorites struck the growing planet at a time when it had become better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have accumulated deep within Earth, eventually becoming part of the planet's enormous internal carbon reservoir.

Over billions of years, carbon from that reservoir could have migrated upward through mantle plumes and emerged in volcanic eruptions.

If the interpretation is correct, some of the carbon essential to life today may have arrived from the outer solar system aboard meteorites during Earth's earliest history.

A Remarkable Journey From Space to Life on Earth.

Despite the intriguing evidence, key questions remain unanswered. The researchers have not conclusively demonstrated that the unusual carbon came from Earth's core or established precisely how much of the planet's carbon was delivered by carbonaceous meteorites.

In a recent development, "We don't really know. We need more measurements," cautions Moussallam.

Nevertheless, the findings offer a fascinating possible connection between the formation of the solar system, the inaccessible depths of our planet, and the carbon that makes life possible.

In a recent development, they also raise the possibility that some of the carbon found in living organisms today has followed an extraordinary path. After arriving on Earth billions of years ago, it may have become incorporated into the planet's metallic core, moved slowly upward through the mantle, and eventually returned to the surface through volcanic eruptions.

In a recent development, "It's fun to think about. We're made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet's core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting.".

In a recent development, the study was coauthored by Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, and Bridgett Holman of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory; Damanveer S. Grewal of Yale University; Estelle F. Rose-Koga of Institut des Sciences de la Terre d'Orléans; Allan Lerner of the US Geological Survey; Paul J. Wallace of the University of Oregon; and Natália Gauer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.

Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.

It has been revealed that "Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November.".

It has been revealed that foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month.

A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.

Industry observers note that in the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a fresh benefits provider.

But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation remarked.

In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated.".

Foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.

The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people remarked.

Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.

The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.

Sources indicate that base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a Upcoming York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.

Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.

The prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.

Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the organization's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.

In a recent development, frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the firm back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak claims that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people noted.

Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some upcoming workers have never been fully paid, said the people.

To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people noted.

At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people said.

Following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the problem in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.

Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people stated.

The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added.

Sources indicate that "I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.
  • The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data indicated with all ballots counted.
  • “We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data indicated with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

“We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister stated in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive new leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

According to recent reports, the NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has noted he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

Industry observers note that the Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

#150701. New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1682 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals.
  • It has been revealed that the discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a upcoming path toward treating conditions that affect the brain.
  • "If we can proceed rapidly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals. The treatment also prevented severe memory decline in mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Remarkably, the approach relies on mRNA technology similar to that used in COVID-19 vaccines.

It has been revealed that the discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a upcoming path toward treating conditions that affect the brain. Potential applications extend beyond Alzheimer's disease to other neurodegenerative disorders, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental conditions.

"If we can proceed rapidly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely said.

In a recent development, the idea behind the research has an unusual origin. The team drew inspiration from Daniel Keyes' science fiction story Flowers for Algernon, which explores the limits of human intelligence through experiments designed to increase intelligence in laboratory mice and people.

How mRNA Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory.

According to recent reports, the treatment works by delivering messenger RNA (mRNA), a type of genetic instruction that tells cells how to produce specific proteins. These instructions are enclosed in tiny fat-based particles called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which protect the mRNA and help it enter cells.

According to recent reports, once delivered through the nose, the mRNA instructs cells to manufacture therapeutic proteins capable of reaching the brain. In effect, the nasal tissue becomes a small drug-producing factory, creating substances that can support brain function.

"In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime," Professor Neely mentioned.

"What's exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic.".

The study, published in Advanced Science, used mRNA to stimulate production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). This naturally occurring protein helps neurons survive, form connections, and adapt as the brain learns and stores memories. Levels of BDNF tend to decline with aging and are also associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The results were striking. Older mice that received the nose drops performed about as well as young mice in standardized tests of working memory, spatial memory, and object recognition. These tests measure abilities such as remembering recently encountered information, navigating surroundings, and recognizing familiar objects. Untreated older animals demonstrated the expected age-related deterioration in cognitive performance.

Nose Drops Prevent Alzheimer's-Like Memory Decline in Mice.

Sources indicate that to investigate whether the treatment might also protect against Alzheimer's disease, researchers turned to a widely used laboratory model known as 5XFAD mice. These animals carry genetic mutations that cause them to develop Alzheimer's-like brain changes and memory problems unusually early in life.

In this model, signs of Alzheimer's-related brain pathology can typically be detected by two months of age, with measurable cognitive decline appearing around four months.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers began administering the BDNF-producing mRNA nose drops when the mice were two months old, around the time the disease-related changes first appeared. Treatment continued twice a week.

According to recent reports, by four months of age, the treated mice revealed no further cognitive decline, unlike the severe deterioration normally seen in this model. The findings suggest that supporting brain cells early in the disease process may help preserve cognitive abilities.

One of the most intriguing results was what the treatment did not do. Although memory and learning were protected, the researchers found no reduction in amyloid plaques, the abnormal protein deposits that accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease.

It has been revealed that that distinction could be important because many existing Alzheimer's treatments aim to remove amyloid. The new approach instead appears to help neurons remain healthy and functional despite the presence of these deposits. If the same effect can eventually be demonstrated in people, the two treatment strategies might be used together.

"Current Alzheimer's treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques," Professor Neely noted. "However, just under a third of Alzheimer's patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it's possible to live with Alzheimer's disease pathology.".

According to recent reports, "Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other.".

Bypassing the Blood-Brain Barrier Through the Nose.

Industry observers note that getting medicines into the brain is one of the biggest obstacles in developing treatments for neurological diseases. The blood-brain barrier acts as a protective filter, preventing many potentially harmful substances in the bloodstream from entering delicate brain tissue. Unfortunately, it also blocks numerous drugs that scientists would like to use to treat brain disorders.

The nose offers a possible alternative route. Connections between the nasal cavity and the central nervous system may allow certain therapeutic substances to reach the brain without requiring surgery or injections directly into the brain or spinal cord.

"This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose," Professor Neely said.

According to recent reports, the team adapted mRNA technology built on the same clinically validated BioNTech platform used for COVID-19 vaccination. Instead of delivering instructions that prompt an immune response, the modified system provides instructions for producing proteins intended to benefit the brain.

First author Dr. Maria Bergamasco, from the University of Sydney's School of Life and Environmental Sciences, explained that the findings illustrate how mRNA technology could be used for purposes far beyond preventing infectious diseases.

Recent findings suggest that "The success of mRNA vaccines revealed these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells," Dr. Bergamasco stated.

"We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way.".

Treatment Stimulates Latest Brain Cell Growth.

Sources indicate that the researchers also detected increased neurogenesis, the process through which new neurons are formed, in the hippocampus. This part of the brain plays an essential role in learning and memory and is particularly vulnerable to damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

In a recent development, the increase in new neurons provides another possible explanation for the improvements in cognitive performance. By promoting the health and adaptability of brain cells, BDNF may help maintain the neural networks needed for learning and remembering information.

The nose drops also appeared to be well tolerated. Researchers reported no major side effects in the mice during the study, although further testing will be needed to establish long-term safety.

Could mRNA Nose Drops Work in Humans?

Recent findings suggest that despite the encouraging results, Professor Neely emphasized that the treatment remains experimental. So far, its effectiveness has been demonstrated only in mice, and additional animal safety studies are required before clinical testing can begin.

It has been revealed that "Before we can trial this therapy in patients, we need to perform a series of safety studies in animals," he stated. "It is a very promising pathway, but human noses are different from mouse noses, so we will need to test our drugs in humans before we know whether it will work.".

That anatomical difference is a significant consideration. A delivery method that successfully transports therapeutic substances from the nasal cavity to the brain in mice may not work in exactly the same way in humans.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, the researchers believe the potential applications could be substantial. Beyond protecting against Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline, the technology might eventually help support memory and other mental abilities during normal aging.

"We believe our upcoming drug, if it works in humans, can promote general cognitive health as people age, should help treat a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, and may even increase cognitive abilities in healthy young people," Professor Neely remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the next steps involve refining the nasal delivery technology and conducting further studies to determine its safety and effectiveness over longer periods. The team hopes to advance toward human clinical trials as swiftly as the required testing allows.

"Based on previous clinical trials, we know the components used in this study to be safe in humans," Professor Neely stated. "We hope we can move quickly through the requisite safety studies and trial this treatment in humans in the next two years.".

Although the individual components have previously been used in humans, the complete nasal treatment still requires its own safety evaluation. Whether it can deliver similar memory benefits in people remains an open question.

Research Funding and Disclosures.

It has been revealed that the project brought together researchers from the Dr. John and Anne Chong Lab for Functional Genomics in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences, the Charles Perkins Centre, and the University of Sydney's Faculty of Medicine and Health.

Sources indicate that greg Neely and Maria Bergamasco are listed as inventors on a provisional patent application associated with the research. The other authors reported no competing interests.

Financial support came from the National Health and Medical Research Council, the NSW Ministry of Health, and an ongoing philanthropic contribution from Dr. John and Anne Chong supporting the Neely Lab's research. The authors also acknowledged the Sydney Imaging Facility for its assistance.

All animal experiments were approved by the University of Sydney Animal Ethics Committee and conducted in accordance with the Australian Code of Practise for the Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes.

According to recent reports, materials provided by University of Sydney. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit.

Atmos, a space tech giant known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle, will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project.

"We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, mentioned in a statement on Nov. 18.

Sources indicate that the system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies noted that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.

Atmos and MBDA also said this work could lead to demonstrations, but the companies' announcement makes it clear that any deployment or use would be subject to the approval of governmental and military authorities.

"The initiative also directly supports MBDA's broader strategic vision in the space domain, reinforcing both space for defense and the defense of space," Thomas Gottschild, MBDA Deutschland managing director, said in the same statement.

In a recent development, this news comes a few months after Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said that the U.S. Space Force operates orbital weapons.

According to recent reports, "Let me be crystal clear: Today, Guardians operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks," Schiess stated during a conferenace presentation on Sept. 15 ("Guardians" refers to Space Force personnel.).

Last year, Atmos' Phoenix capsule got its first test run in space. The cargo-return technology launched aboard a Space X Falcon 9 rocket during a rideshare mission in February 2025.

Atmos tested out the inflatable heat shields it has been working on to help future space-manufactured cargo make it through Earth's atmosphere in one piece.

"Orbital transportation and return form a new layer of strategic infrastructure, and infrastructure determines what Europe can achieve on its own terms," Klaus noted in the Nov 18 statement.

Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Queensland have demonstrated an unusual newly introduced way to communicate, using gravity to send a message directly through a brick wall.
  • Sources indicate that the experiment took place inside UQ's Parnell Building.
  • According to recent reports, on the other side of a brick wall, a device called a gravimeter was positioned in a nearby bathroom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Queensland have demonstrated an unusual newly introduced way to communicate, using gravity to send a message directly through a brick wall. Instead of relying on radio waves or other electromagnetic signals, the team used an old elevator, a massive counterweight, and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in gravitational pull.

Sources indicate that the experiment took place inside UQ's Parnell Building. Physicists repeatedly moved an elevator between two floors, shifting its 1.8-metric-ton counterweight between two positions. Each position represented a binary digit, either 0 or 1, allowing the researchers to encode information through the movement of the heavy mass.

According to recent reports, on the other side of a brick wall, a device called a gravimeter was positioned in a nearby bathroom. The instrument measured the extremely small changes in gravity produced by the moving counterweight. By decoding those measurements, the team successfully recovered a one-word message: 'Gravity'.

Why Gravity Could Succeed Where Wi-Fi Fails.

According to recent reports, the experiment highlights a potentially important advantage of using gravity for communication. Unlike conventional wireless signals, which can be weakened or blocked by physical obstacles, gravitational fields pass through ordinary materials without being screened out.

Dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ's School of Mathematics and Physics explained why this property makes gravity an intriguing alternative to existing communication technologies.

"Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," Dr. Woffinden said.

"Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

"While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.".

Recent findings suggest that the basic principle is surprisingly simple. Any object with mass produces a gravitational field, and moving that object changes the field around it. Although these changes are generally far too small for people to notice, sufficiently sensitive instruments can detect them. By controlling how a large mass moves, researchers can create a sequence of gravitational changes that represents digital information.

From Weighing Trucks to Sending Messages.

The idea for the experiment emerged from a separate research effort that had little to do with communication.

Dr. Andrew Groszek noted the team had originally been developing a contactless weighbridge, a system designed to measure the weight of vehicles without requiring them to drive onto a conventional scale.

"We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull," Dr. Groszek said.

"Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.".

It has been revealed that that realization opened the door to a different application. If a sensitive detector could measure the gravitational influence of a large vehicle, it could also detect deliberately controlled changes in the position of a heavy object. Those changes could then be used to represent the ones and zeros that form the foundation of digital communication.

Despite its success, the demonstration revealed a major obstacle to practical gravity-based communication: transmitting information this way is extraordinarily slow.

Professor Andrew White explained that the elevator's age and limited speed placed a severe restriction on how swiftly the researchers could send their message.

"Our lift was snail-paced - it's from the 1950s - so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," Professor White stated.

For comparison, a bit is the smallest unit of digital information, representing either a 0 or a 1. Modern communication systems transmit enormous numbers of bits every second. The gravity experiment, by contrast, required an entire minute to communicate just one bit.

According to White, improving the system would require finding ways to produce detectable gravitational changes more rapidly.

"The speed of gravity communication would come down to how major the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.

"It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.".

Could Quantum Sensors Make Gravity Communication Practical?

Although the experiment relied on a conventional gravity sensor, the researchers believe more advanced technology could eventually make the approach faster and capable of operating over greater distances.

Professor Matthew Davis emphasized that the team's most notable achievement was demonstrating that gravity could be used to transmit recoverable information.

"It's not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely fresh way of communicating," Professor Davis said.

"We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

"Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.".

Quantum sensors exploit properties of quantum physics to make exceptionally precise measurements. In principle, their greater sensitivity could allow researchers to detect much smaller gravitational changes, potentially improving both the range and speed of gravity-based communication.

However, the team's projections depend on ambitious assumptions, and the suggested performance has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. Even at 15 bits per minute, the system would remain dramatically slower than modern wireless technologies.

Recent findings suggest that still, the potential applications are intriguing. A sufficiently advanced gravity-based communication system could someday transmit information in environments where radio waves, light, and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

For now, an aging elevator and a gravimeter in a university bathroom have demonstrated something remarkable: information can be carried by changes in gravity and recovered on the other side of a solid wall.

The research was published in Science Advances.

NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa
