📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth.
  • According to recent reports, recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers.
  • While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

According to recent reports, recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly key as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A latest investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

Industry observers note that but looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

Many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

Before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.

The researchers found that while the plants highlighted some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

Researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station.

Menu fatigue can swiftly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something new and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space.

In a recent development, NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

#150694. AI goes from math dunce to genius

AI goes from math dunce to genius

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions.
  • A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised.
  • Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence firm Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions. Thankfully, I double-checked. The total was wrong by a few pounds.

A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised. Chatbots, he mentioned, often get simple calculations wrong.

Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence firm Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.

That problem was the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and has baffled mathematicians since 1859.

How did AI go from stumbling over simple arithmetic to scaling such extraordinary mathematical heights?

The answer lies in how AI processes information, said Andrea Asperti, a professor in computer science at Italy's University of Bologna.

Unlike conventional calculators, early chatbots were trained to predict language, producing plausible answers without necessarily doing the math.

Ironically, they may perform millions of calculations to arrive at the wrong answer.

"In a sense, asking why a chatbot makes arithmetic mistakes despite its enormous computational power is like asking why humans make mistakes in mental arithmetic despite having billions of neurons in their brains," Asperti told DW.

Ken Ono, a mathematics professor at the University of Virginia in the United States, recalled how Google's Gemini once concluded that 9.11 was greater than 9.8.

"But make no mistake, those errors are very rare today," Ono told DW.

Asperti attributed AI's gains to gradual improvements in model size, training data and methods rather than a single breakthrough.

AI can now explore different approaches, check its work, correct mistakes and use specialized computational tools.

"What is remarkable is that these relatively incremental technological improvements have resulted in qualitative leaps in intellectual capabilities," Asperti mentioned.

Perhaps most surprising was AI's ability to solve previously unsolved problems — something many had doubted it could do.

"Solving open mathematical problems requires a considerable degree of creativity: it is not simply a matter of retrieving existing knowledge or reproducing known arguments," Asperti noted.

Kevin Buzzard, a mathematician at Imperial College London, UK, was excited but not surprised by the proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis.

He had already seen AI resolve a problem in algebraic geometry by finding a counterexample.

"I had thought about the problem myself and could see what the difficulties were. AI cut through them," Buzzard told DW.

Recent findings suggest that ono draws an analogy with chess: While humans struggle to think several moves ahead, AI can explore countless possibilities. In advanced mathematics, the scope is far greater.

"When it comes to pure mathematics, there are tens of thousands of research papers that are the individual moves that it gets to play with. And what we're seeing is the power of that capacity," Ono noted.

Another advantage is AI's ability to recognize connections across different areas of mathematics.

In a recent development, "Most of us become specialists, building upon theories that we learn over time. And it's difficult to become proficient in many more than a small handful of areas," Ono remarked.

The proposed Riemann proof illustrates that breadth. "It might be 30 or 40 mathematicians you would have to put in a room before you could assemble this proof," he said.

And AI's knowledge extends well beyond math.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that ono suggested that the mathematician behind the Claude-assisted proof could have interrupted his work to ask the chatbot: "Hey, by the way, next week I'm going to Hawaii. Come up with a beautiful itinerary for a long weekend in Hawaii.".

He and Claude could then have seamlessly returned to advanced mathematics.

"The point I make there is that Claude seems to know everything at a fairly deep level, and humans don't," Ono said.

Ono suggests the individual ideas behind the proposed proof may all be within human intellectual reach.

"But the sheer scope and the ability to assemble ideas that had never been assembled before, that is what is extraordinary here," he mentioned.

Ono called the achievement "superhuman.".

Asperti believes AI could develop an entirely different kind of mathematical intuition.

Mathematicians work with abstract spaces of hundreds or thousands of dimensions, which humans, living in a three-dimensional world, struggle to visualize.

AI might develop its own ways of understanding such structures and "discover relationships that are difficult for us even to imagine," Asperti said.

Ono is excited about the future of mathematics but concerned about the future of mathematicians.

Until recently, he would have discouraged young mathematicians from tackling problems like the Riemann hypothesis, saying they could spend 20 years without producing any results.

Recent findings suggest that "Shoot for the moon! The bar has been raised so high that if your primary interest as a mathematician is in the questions themselves, then this is a great time.".

"The flip side, if you're a mathematician and your identity is that you want to be the source of the ideas, well, you may have lost most of that.".

Ono, who has trained 35 PhD students, is "deeply worried" about their future.

Industry observers note that "Make no mistake. In the year 2026, the ground shifted beneath the entire edifice of the world of human mathematical research," he said.

Ono believes the role of future mathematicians will be "much more like being a conductor of the most extraordinary orchestra.".

In the past, mathematicians were trained by getting them to prove theorems.

"Now you can prove a theorem by pressing a button," said Buzzard, "so we need fresh methods.".

Buzzard is setting up a lab that emphasizes understanding, explaining and defending complex mathematical arguments.

"The best team for doing mathematics is a computer plus human team, and it is still relatively straightforward to extract insights and understanding from what machines are doing," he remarked.

But, he mentioned, mathematical research may "end up completely dominated by machines doing things which humans simply cannot comprehend any more, very cheaply and at the touch of a button.".

So, that is the issue of solving mathematical problems. What about AI's ability to come up with mathematical problems and propositions, like an Albert Einstein?

According to recent reports, ono remarked: "If you trained a large language model on all the mathematics and all the physics that was known by the end of the 19th century, would a model spin up Einstein's theory of relativity on its own? I don't think we've seen that sort of creative spark, that sort of ability yet.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that how NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA declared its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Organization and GRACE Aerospace.

According to recent reports, NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

“We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”.

According to recent reports, under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

In a recent development, “Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” stated Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”.

Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

“GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” mentioned Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”.

NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

https://www.nasa.gov/osbp/supplier-development-program/.

#150686. Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1397 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, about 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again.
  • The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a latest ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.
  • Industry observers note that "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," indicates Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, about 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to upcoming research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a latest ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.

Industry observers note that "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," indicates Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.".

Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History.

In a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago.

At its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains.

Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware.

"People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," indicates Young.

Recent findings suggest that scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again.

Answering that question could reveal whether a latest cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed.

(A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.).

Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues.

It has been revealed that piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading.

The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history.

It has been revealed that unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

It has been revealed that since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating.

This technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice.

These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape.

It has been revealed that "If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," says Young.

Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago.

The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region.

Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change.

Industry observers note that their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.

Young and his colleagues argue that this renewed growth should be recognized as the start of Earth's next glacial period.

That interpretation differs from previous research based on climate models, which has generally suggested that the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

Sources indicate that the disagreement partly comes down to how scientists define the beginning of a glacial period. Rather than waiting until enormous ice sheets have spread across continents, Young's team proposes that the first sustained expansion of an existing ice sheet should mark the starting point.

Under that definition, the next glaciation had already begun long before modern scientists recognized it.

The discovery also casts newly introduced light on a controversial scientific debate from the 1970s, when some climate researchers suggested that another ice age might be approaching.

"It actually was happening," Young claims. "They couldn't quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence.".

However, this early expansion would not have produced an immediate or dramatic transformation of the planet. According to Young, it would have taken thousands of years for the cooling to become noticeable and roughly 30,000 years for the Laurentide Ice Sheet to regain its enormous continental dimensions.

The process was only in its earliest stages when the warming climate brought it to a halt.

Global Warming Reversed the Growth of the Ice Sheet.

By the 1960s, conditions had changed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during the summer than it could replace through winter snowfall.

Instead of continuing to expand, the ancient ice began shrinking.

According to the researchers' interpretation, this reversal effectively ended the developing glacial period before it could progress into a full-scale ice age.

It has been revealed that the consequences may extend far beyond the present day. Models projecting the future of the Barnes Ice Cap indicate that it could disappear entirely within the next few centuries.

"That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young notes.

The Loss of an Ancient Ice Cap Could Change Future Ice Ages.

The disappearance of the Barnes Ice Cap could also have implications for how future glacial periods develop.

In the past, the Laurentide Ice Sheet provided a starting point for renewed glaciation whenever Earth's climate cooled sufficiently. Because a large existing mass of ice helps create conditions favorable for further ice accumulation, it can trigger reinforcing processes that allow glaciers to expand.

Scientists describe this kind of process as a positive feedback. In this case, existing ice helps promote the growth of additional ice, allowing an ice sheet to become increasingly extensive as temperatures remain cold.

Without the Laurentide's last surviving remnant, a future glacial period might unfold differently.

Researchers cannot yet determine when another glaciation could begin under atmospheric conditions influenced by elevated greenhouse gas concentrations. If enormous continental ice sheets eventually start forming again, they may have to develop without the ancient ice that previously helped initiate their growth.

It has been revealed that the findings suggest that global warming has done more than melt glaciers and shrink existing ice sheets. It may have interrupted a glacial cycle that was already beginning, while also removing a feature that helped sustain ice age cycles across North America for millions of years.

"What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone," indicates Young.

Tech Report: How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.
  • According to recent reports, that's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977.
  • In a recent development, A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.

According to recent reports, that's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977. But what led to this?

In a recent development, A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany. Unlike West Germany's Deutsche Mark, the East German Mark was a domestic currency with no value abroad.

Even under normal circumstances, the country constantly struggled to obtain the hard currency it needed to pay for imports. In 1974 and 1975, East Germany spent around 150 million Valutamarks — the term used in East Germany for the West German Deutsche Mark — on imported coffee. The following year, it had to pay almost five times as much.

However, this rate of inflation could not be passed on to consumers because, "In the GDR, there was the dogma of stable prices — set by the state through law," explains historian Stefan Wolle, a consultant at the DDR Museum in Berlin (DDR is the acronym used for East Germany in German). "Prices were set by the Politburo, not by businesses. And they weren't allowed to change. What sounds wonderfully socially minded at first glance had serious negative economic consequences, because production costs were far higher than retail prices.".

It has been revealed that the government needed a solution. On August 1, 1977, it introduced "Kaffee Mix" as a substitute for popular coffee brands back then such as Kosta, Rondo and Mocca Fix. The fine print on the packaging promised "a blend of select green coffee beans and carefully balanced coffee substitutes.".

In plain English, that meant 51% of the blend consisted of imported coffee beans. The rest was a mixture of rye and barley, along with chicory and either spelt or sugar beet. It tasted disgusting, Wolle recalls.

Industry observers note that even the coffee machines appeared to reject the concoction. The mixture expanded and clogged the filters in cafeterias and restaurants. Some machines were even said to have exploded.

Public discontent boiled over during this "coffee crisis." People responded by boycotting the product, and with biting sarcasm, too: "The difference between a neutron bomb and coffee mix: There isn't one — the cup stays intact, but the person is destroyed.".

It has been revealed that A sharper dig? "It's pure rat poison.".

In a recent development, more than 14,000 complaint letters poured into government offices. On September 1, the Ministry for State Security, better known as the Stasi, reported to the leadership of the ruling Socialist Unity Party of Germany or SED, that Kaffee Mix was being "rejected by broad sections of the population." (Editor's note: The SED was the only ruling party in East Germany then).

To understand the intensity of the backlash, it's crucial to recognize coffee's special place in East German society.

"Coffee was, in a way, the social glue that held together East Germany's particular brand of conviviality and camaraderie," states Wolle.

In a recent development, during the 1960s and 1970s, people would gather for coffee after lunch, often accompanied by homemade cakes or treats from the bakery. "It was a sacred hour in every workplace and office. It was a huge mistake for the SED leadership to slaughter this sacred cow, so to speak.".

Industry observers note that according to Wolle, real coffee was still occasionally available in the larger cities. But in smaller towns and rural areas, people often had no choice but to make do with Kaffee Mix. East Germans who had relatives or friends in West Germany and regularly received packages from them could count themselves lucky.

"Our relatives and friends in the West knew what was in short supply in East Germany, so they would usually include a big bag of good West German coffee," Wolle recalls.

Recent findings suggest that it is estimated that around 25% of all coffee consumed in East Germany came from the West. During the height of the coffee crisis, that share was briefly even higher.

In a recent development, "Of course, the SED leadership had mixed feelings about people receiving so many packages from the West," Wolle states. "Police officers and full-time party officials weren't allowed to have contacts in the West. But ordinary citizens didn't care.".

Especially after the blend stirred up such negative reactions.

East Germany's leaders responded by looking to their socialist allies in Africa for help. They negotiated special agreements with Angola and Ethiopia.

It has been revealed that "Instead of paying in hard currency, they paid with military equipment — weapons and trucks," Wolle explains. "Weapons that were used in Ethiopia's civil war.".

But the East German leadership sought a long-term solution, and eventually established a partnership with another socialist ally: Vietnam.

"Coffee had already been grown there under French colonial rule," says Wolle. "People knew that coffee grew well there and that the quality was good.".

According to recent reports, starting in the 1980s, East Germany invested heavily in developing the infrastructure needed for large-scale coffee cultivation in Vietnam, Wolle explains. It supplied machinery and equipment, built transportation routes, and provided housing for plantation workers. "There was just one catch: Coffee plants take several years before they can be harvested.".

By the time the plants were finally ready to produce coffee, the Berlin Wall had fallen and East Germany was a thing of the past.

In a recent development, "But the Vietnamese benefited enormously," indicates Wolle. "They converted the plantations into private enterprises fairly quickly." Today, Vietnam is one of the world's largest coffee exporters. "What's surprising is that most people don't even know that.".

There’s no mention of it on the packages — and if there is, it’s in microscopic print.

"The Vietnamese don’t make a big deal out of their role because they themselves probably still believe that coffee has to come from Brazil — or at least from Latin America — to be any good," notes Wolle.

Passionate coffee drinkers may not care where the hot beverage comes from — as long as it doesn't taste like spelt and sugar beets, as the much-maligned East German Kaffee Mix once did.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that in the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in Fresh Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

It has been revealed that in the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in Fresh Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers.

It has been revealed that resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.”.

In a recent development, so began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō, and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park. This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean.

The uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula.

Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “landmark effort,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby.

In 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution.

Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget prepares by former Prime Minister Liz Truss.
  • In a recent development, sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022.
  • Industry observers note that the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget prepares by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

In a recent development, sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

Industry observers note that the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

This resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled looks to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” stated Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a big re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole noted.

According to recent reports, the euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Industry observers note that jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, remarked he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s prepares and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. #150678. 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1205 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea.
  • Industry observers note that for as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms.
  • Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

Industry observers note that for as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a fresh study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

"In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," stated first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship.".

Ancient Waterproofing Secrets Revealed.

It has been revealed that since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

"Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions.".

To uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax.

Sources indicate that the team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

Industry observers note that one sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

The addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past.

In a recent development, the sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

In a recent development, different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

In a recent development, the pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

The discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean.

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

The stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

Sources indicate that earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an crucial maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

Sources indicate that the new pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

According to recent reports, the findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

It has been revealed that "While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical.".

No shade to Vancelette, who got little to do in the role of Vicky. But if any Yellowjacket was going to get a mom played by a movie idol of the '80s, it ought to be Van. What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory.
  • Sources indicate that hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades.
  • Industry observers note that like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory. Researchers propose that the brain not only communicates through electrical signals but may also "write" and "read" memories through chemical interactions involving neurons, astrocytes, and the molecules surrounding them. By linking memory to emotion and thought, the theory raises an increasingly relevant question: Can computational power alone give rise to the kind of consciousness experienced by living organisms?

Sources indicate that hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades. A distinctive scent can bring a forgotten person or place to mind, while recalling a terrifying experience can trigger both emotional and physical reactions within moments.

Industry observers note that like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information. However, the mechanisms underlying biological memory may be fundamentally different.

A new review by Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Professor Chaim Gilon of the Department of Chemistry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem explores the physical and chemical mechanisms that could link memory, emotion, and thought.

In their paper, "Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective," the researchers suggest that understanding memory requires more than studying neurons and their electrical activity. They argue that other brain cells, particularly astrocytes, and the intricate molecular environment surrounding them may also play essential roles.

Building on their previous research into the molecular foundations of memory, Marx and Gilon examine whether the processes responsible for storing and retrieving experiences could also shed light on the origins of intelligence, thought, and consciousness.

The Brain's Hidden Chemical Code for Memory.

Central to the researchers' proposal is a model known as the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory.

According to this theory, memories emerge from interactions between three major components: brain cells, especially astrocytes working alongside neurons; the molecular substances surrounding those cells; and various chemicals, including metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

Rather than relying exclusively on electrical communication between neurons, the brain may use chemical processes to encode and retrieve information.

Industry observers note that astrocytes, which are abundant throughout the brain and maintain close interactions with neurons, are particularly important to this proposed mechanism. Marx and Gilon suggest that groups of astrocytes help process cognitive information through their interactions with neurons and the extracellular environment, the space and molecular material surrounding brain cells.

The new paper expands this hypothesis to explore the nature of thought itself. If the brain can physically encode an experience as a memory, the process of recovering that information, recognizing it, and interpreting its significance might contribute to the formation of thoughts.

Why Memories Carry Emotional Meaning.

One of the central arguments of the researchers' theory is that biological memories contain more than stored information. They are also closely connected to emotional experiences.

In a recent development, A scent associated with childhood may spark feelings of happiness. Hearing a familiar voice can provide reassurance, while remembering a frightening event may produce an immediate physical response.

Industry observers note that marx and Gilon contend that a physical model of memory must account for these emotional associations. Their proposed mechanism incorporates neurotransmitters and other chemical messengers that may help encode cognitive information alongside its emotional significance.

This potential biochemical connection between memory and emotion provides a starting point for investigating larger questions about how the brain generates thought, intelligence, and conscious experiences.

What Human Consciousness May Have That AI Lacks.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence makes these ideas particularly relevant.

According to recent reports, although computers and brains can both retain and access information, the physical mechanisms behind these abilities may differ considerably. Computer memory is ultimately encoded in electronic hardware. Biological memory, the researchers propose, may instead depend on the intricate cellular and chemical machinery of living brain tissue.

This distinction becomes increasingly significant as AI systems grow more capable of performing tasks traditionally associated with human reasoning and intelligence.

Sources indicate that marx and Gilon challenge the assumption that simply increasing computational power and complexity will eventually produce consciousness comparable to that of a living brain. They argue that electronic systems lack the biological structures and emotional mechanisms found in living organisms.

The researchers are not suggesting that AI cannot develop increasingly advanced intellectual capabilities. Instead, they question whether demonstrating intelligent behavior is equivalent to possessing the biological mechanisms responsible for memory, emotion, and conscious experience.

How Memory May Give Rise to Thought.

In a recent development, marx and Gilon emphasize that their theory does not solve the enduring mystery of consciousness. They explicitly acknowledge that the nature of conscious life remains poorly understood.

Recent findings suggest that however, their proposed biochemical framework offers a different way to investigate the physical processes that may underlie mental activity. By examining interactions between brain cells and their chemical environment, the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory could provide researchers with another avenue for exploring how the mind works.

While their earlier research focused on how memories might be physically encoded within the brain, their latest work addresses a much broader problem.

Understanding how living brain tissue transforms experience into memory could eventually help explain how memories become thoughts, how conscious experiences arise, and what fundamentally distinguishes biological intelligence from artificial intelligence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the Covid-19 pandemic, Greg Silverman watched an MTA bus driver pull over on Manhattan's Upper West Side, let his passengers off and run across the street toward him.

Industry observers note that silverman, who runs Newly introduced York nonprofit West Side Campaign Against Hunger, initially thought the driver wanted to use the bathroom at the church where the food distribution was taking place. Instead, the man asked, "Can I get some food?".

Recent findings suggest that "He was a full-time employee," Silverman stated. "You are an essential personnel, making the city survive and you need food.".

Now, Silverman said, his organization has seen demand surpass even the levels it observed during that time of crisis when the U.S. economy ground to a halt — and many of the people now seeking food also have jobs. Silverman expects the nonprofit to distribute as much as 6 million pounds of food this year.

"The height of the pandemic was not the height of need, by any means," he said.

It has been revealed that the pressure on the emergency food system extends beyond Upcoming York. Nationally, use of charitable food programs remains elevated as sustained inflation makes it harder for Americans to afford food, housing and healthcare. Higher prices come at the same time that the federal government has restricted food aid.

The Department of Agriculture's latest annual report found that 13.7% of U.S. households, roughly 18.3 million households, experienced food insecurity in 2024. That rate was significantly higher than in every year from 2016 through 2021.

The pandemic initially brought a surge in demand for charitable food programs, which was followed by government support. In the years that followed, pandemic-era policies such as expanded Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits, the enhanced child tax credit and school meal programs phased out as inflation spiked.

It has been revealed that "This is not because you can't go to work," remarked City Harvest President Carlos Rodriguez. "Primarily, your work and your wages are just not keeping up with the way costs have gone up in the last five years alone.".

Sources indicate that city Harvest, which works with food providers across the five boroughs of Fresh York, told CNBC 1 in 5 New Yorkers is currently experiencing food insecurity, or limited access to enough food because of a lack of money or other resources. That is up from 1 in 6 a year earlier, and 1 in 8 before the pandemic.

Average monthly visits to food pantries and soup kitchens in New York are also 85% higher than before the pandemic, stated Rodriguez.

Industry observers note that in the Federal Reserve's October Beige Book, the central bank's New York regional branch described a sharp rise in first-time food pantry users. One nonprofit leader told the Federal Reserve Bank of New York that the strain was comparable to the pandemic, "but without the same philanthropic and government support.".

Data from Plentiful, a technology platform that connects people with food pantries and tracks their usage, also points to growing demand and limited resources.

According to recent reports, "For pantries using our reservation and pre-registration features, we see that the overwhelming majority of those are at or over capacity," remarked Catherine Compitello, CEO of Plentiful. "Demand is growing while supply is not.".

First-time users of Plentiful in New York City rose roughly 56% from August to October, Compitello said. It was the second-largest fall surge since 2016; the only larger one came during last year's federal government shutdown, when delayed SNAP benefits drove more people to seek food assistance.

Compitello said that when families have trouble affording essentials, they often prioritize healthcare, transportation, childcare and utilities, leaving food as the expense they cut back on.

Demand for food banks is rising in other regions of the country, and nonprofits are facing their own operational challenges as they try to meet it.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank told CNBC the organization's diesel bill more than doubled in September, to roughly $75,000, adding to the cost of delivering food and running refrigerated trucks.

Industry observers note that demand in the region is also spiking. Distribution in the Los Angeles area for January through September totaled 116 million pounds of food and grocery products — the equivalent of 93 million meals — and slightly higher than a near-record year in 2025, according to the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank.

Sources indicate that federal food aid changes have exacerbated the problems. Rodriguez of City Harvest described SNAP as a first line of defense against hunger, saying the program can provide as many as nine meals for every one meal the organization provides. But City Harvest has estimated at least 8.7% of SNAP recipients in Upcoming York City lost benefits over the past year, after congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump approved work certification requirements and changes to eligibility.

According to recent reports, the pressure is also mounting in Los Angeles County, where roughly 260,000 CalFresh recipients are subject to expanded federal work requirements that took effect in June. CalFresh is California's version of SNAP.

Recent findings suggest that that does not mean all 260,000 will lose benefits, since people who meet the work requirements or qualify for an exemption can remain eligible. But a Los Angeles Regional Food Bank spokesperson told CNBC the changes add another layer of uncertainty for households already struggling with food costs.

In Atlanta, the pressure extends beyond the city itself to the surrounding region. The Atlanta Community Food Bank serves about 270,000 households a month, or nearly 700,000 people, through partner pantries across North Georgia. President and CEO Kyle Waide said the number of people it serves has jumped more than 70% in five years.

"Much of that increase is among people whose incomes are too high to qualify for federal benefit programs," noted Waide.

Under current SNAP guidelines in Georgia, most households must have gross monthly income at or below 130% of the federal poverty level to qualify. They must also meet a separate net income test. For fiscal 2027, which began Oct. 1, the gross income limit is $2,960 a month for a household of three, or about $35,520 annually, and $3,575 a month for a household of four, or $42,900 a year.

In a recent development, more than 60% of Atlanta Community Food Bank clients have household incomes above the cutoff for SNAP eligibility, Waide stated, generally in the mid-to-upper $30,000 range depending on household size. The food bank does not collect everyone's income, he said, but the figure is based on survey estimates.

Given those dynamics, Waide noted he does not expect the need to ease.

"We're preparing for the level of demand to stay where it is today, or even increase more," Waide said. "We don't see a big source of relief coming anytime soon.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A cloud layer encircled the flanks of the volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula but left its restless summit caldera in view.

It has been revealed that in the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes.

The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome, formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows.

Industry observers note that in November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months, according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). And despite frequent cloudiness, satellites regularly detect thermal anomalies from the volcano.

On the day of this image, KVERT reported that a plume of resuspended ash drifted 120 kilometers (75 miles) to the east. That kind of activity is relatively tame for the mountain. Explosions from Shivelyuch periodically send ash several kilometers up into the atmosphere, where it can travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft. In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, according to news reports, prompting the cancellation of multiple flights.

According to recent reports, NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, physicists at Northwestern University have achieved an unprecedented level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists answer one of the most fundamental questions in physics: Why does the universe exist as we know it?

According to recent reports, the researchers captured a rapidly moving positron produced through radioactive decay, slowed it down, and cooled it to a temperature just above absolute zero. They then confined the particle within a near-perfect vacuum, isolating it from ordinary matter, which would cause it to annihilate.

Using this approach, the team created what they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." Within this system, the positron behaves somewhat like an artificial atom, allowing researchers to observe and precisely manipulate its individual quantum energy levels.

Recent findings suggest that the achievement lays the groundwork for what could become the most rigorous test yet of the fundamental symmetry between electrons and positrons. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that the two particles should behave as nearly perfect mirror images of each other.

It has been revealed that by measuring the positron's magnetic properties with unprecedented accuracy and comparing them with those of an electron, scientists could uncover previously undetected differences. Any unexpected discrepancy would point to a weakness in the Standard Model and potentially offer clues to why the universe contains so much more matter than antimatter.

The research was published in Physical Review Letters.

Recent findings suggest that "Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction," said Northwestern's Gerald Gabrielse, who led the study. "If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers' imaginations. The major mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we'd be left with nothing. There's clearly something wrong with that theory, and that's what we're trying to figure out.".

Industry observers note that gabrielse is the Board of Trustees Professor of Physics at Northwestern's Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and director of the university's Center for Fundamental Physics. Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student working in Gabrielse's laboratory, is the study's first author.

Searching for Cracks in the Standard Model.

Industry observers note that the Standard Model is one of the most successful theories in modern science. It describes the universe's fundamental particles and three of its four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces). Countless experiments have verified its predictions with remarkable accuracy.

Recent findings suggest that despite those successes, the theory remains incomplete. One of its most significant shortcomings is its inability to explain the overwhelming abundance of matter compared with antimatter in the observable universe.

"We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere -- or at least incomplete," Gabrielse said. "For example, it cannot predict why the universe exists, so that's a pretty major loophole. We're very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down. We hope to find an unambiguous answer.".

Gabrielse has devoted decades of his scientific career to investigating this mystery. His research group previously developed methods for isolating individual electrons and determining their magnetic properties with exceptional precision.

It has been revealed that he also helped establish the field of low-energy antimatter research by pioneering techniques for slowing, capturing, and cooling antiprotons. The latest achievement combines these two areas of expertise, extending the sophisticated quantum control previously demonstrated with electrons to an individual antimatter particle.

Trapping Antimatter Without Touching It.

Almost everything on Earth is composed of three familiar particles: electrons, protons, and neutrons. A universe made of antimatter could contain their respective counterparts: positrons, antiprotons, and antineutrons. According to Gabrielse, if everything on Earth were constructed from antimatter instead of ordinary matter, distinguishing between the two would be remarkably difficult.

The dramatic differences emerge when matter and antimatter come into contact. An electron and a positron, for example, can annihilate when they encounter one another. This makes storing antimatter particularly challenging, as contact with the material walls of an ordinary container would almost certainly destroy the trapped particle.

"If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully," Gabrielse noted. "To be clear, it's not dangerous. We don't have enough antimatter to make an explosion.".

To overcome this problem, the Northwestern researchers employed an advanced particle trap that uses carefully configured electric and magnetic fields. These fields keep the positron suspended in an empty region of space, preventing it from coming into contact with the surrounding material.

By effectively creating a container that does not require the particle to touch any physical walls, the team has managed to keep a single positron confined in Gabrielse's laboratory for months.

Cooling Antimatter to Near Absolute Zero.

Capturing a positron presents another considerable technical hurdle. Certain atomic nuclei release positrons as they undergo radioactive decay. For their experiment, the researchers used sodium-22, a rare radioactive isotope of sodium. Positrons emitted during this process initially carry tremendous amounts of energy.

Industry observers note that the physicists substantially reduced the particle's speed before directing it into the trap's near-perfect vacuum. Inside, the temperature is maintained at approximately 300 millikelvins, equivalent to just 0.3 degrees above absolute zero.

Under these extremely cold conditions, the positron can settle into its lowest possible quantum energy state.

"We cool it down so much that it's in its quantum ground state," Gabrielse stated. "We actually coaxed this very fast positron to sit there and behave for months at a time.".

Putting Matter and Antimatter to the Ultimate Test.

Beyond capturing and cooling the positron, the researchers demonstrated that they could deliberately change its individual quantum energy states and detect those changes.

According to recent reports, using microwaves tuned to specific frequencies, the physicists transferred carefully controlled amounts of energy to the particle and observed the resulting transitions between quantum states. This ability is crucial to their larger objective of determining the positron's magnetic properties with exceptional accuracy and comparing them directly with those of an electron.

It has been revealed that in earlier research, Gabrielse and his colleagues used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to determine the electron's magnetic moment, a measure of its magnetic properties, with a precision of approximately one part in 10 trillion. That achievement ranks among the most precise measurements ever performed on an elementary particle.

Recent findings suggest that the team now intends to conduct an equivalent measurement using the trapped positron. Comparing the two results could provide an extraordinarily sensitive test of current particle physics theories and potentially uncover evidence of previously unknown physics.

"Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements," Gabrielse remarked. "If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century.".

The study, "One-positron quantum cyclotron," received support from the National Science Foundation (grant number 2110565).

Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.

Sources indicate that the consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The company said that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about.".

Industry observers note that best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.

The earnings report is the firm's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.

Bonfig noted the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game rolls out and a targeted product assortment.

Looking ahead into the holiday season, he stated the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can.

"We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more latest customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig said. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year.".

Here's how the firm performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Recent findings suggest that best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.

Recent findings suggest that revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.

Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs.

Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year.

Bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy launched a newly introduced gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features.

"I think there'll still be opportunities for gaming to continue to drive our business moving forward," Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday.
