Tech Report: Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.
  • Sources indicate that the shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop.
  • That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.

Sources indicate that the shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop. The U.S. secondhand apparel market grew 13% in 2025, nearly four times faster than the overall retail clothing market, according to GlobalData.

That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found. Much of that expansion — 40% — was driven by Generation Z, followed closely by millennials.

"I think this has been their version of the thrill of the hunt that millennials loved during the recession days," Katherine Cullen, a global senior retail analyst at EY, told CNBC. "It's a way to really express an individual style, find something unique, something that really fits their own vibe and personality.".

According to recent reports, it goes beyond people shopping for themselves, Cullen said. With more emphasis on unique holiday gifts, shoppers are leaning more on secondhand retail than they have before, whether in clothing or in other retail categories.

They're looking for something that fits the personality of the person they're shopping for, she added.

For Vanessa Roberts, that meant finding two antique children's chairs that she says will perfectly round out her nieces' play space. Roberts, 37, stated she's been thrifting for at least two decades, each time embracing the "thrill" of finding something unique or vintage.

Especially in fashion, at a time when the quality of mass-produced items has decreased, thrifted items offer more value beyond just the price tag, Roberts added.

"It's crazy that you can find better quality items at the thrift store right now from 20 years ago versus what you can find at stores right now," she stated.

Sources indicate that roberts, who lives in Los Angeles, said she began shopping for holiday gifts in September. As she prepares her haul for December, roughly 70% of her gifting will come from secondhand stores, she estimated.

In a recent development, "It's been a fun little challenge, where it's like a little scavenger hunt when I go into the thrift store," she noted. "I'm definitely thrifting for the holidays – I do it every year.".

The trend coincides with an economy that has forced consumers to be more intentional about how they spend, as they face high inflation and elevated gas prices.

In October, the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, which was more than anticipated. Still, consumers are expected to continue spending through the holiday season, with sales projected to top $1 trillion for the first time — though some of that estimated increase is boosted by inflation.

"You have a consumer who, while they're willing to spend at the top level, they're willing to splurge selectively," Cullen said. "Consumers are looking for value, which I think is something that is making secondhand resale and re-commerce more attractive.".

And while clothing is largely the entry point to buying resale, secondhand shopping is increasingly expanding into furniture, electronics and books, according to a report from consumer insights firm The Consumer Collective.

Its October report found that 34% of people surveyed mentioned secondhand products offer better value than brand new ones.

Many secondhand items also have an inherent added value beyond the low price on the tag, according to eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. The uniqueness of those products, as well as the allure that vintage adds to them, means consumers may actually be seeking the benefits of secondhand in more ways than one.

Sources indicate that "I can buy a product that's used, and it almost has cachet around it," Iannone told CNBC. "Consumers today, they're able to get these amazing values on products, and it's seen as very normal to be gifting pre-loved.".

According to eBay's Recommerce Report in October, 70% of global consumers surveyed said they consider secondhand shopping important for managing their budgets. That same report also found that 89% of respondents proposal to spend the same amount or more on secondhand products next year compared with this year.

Iannone stated he thinks the interest in secondhand this holiday season is "much stronger" than last year.

"It's becoming just a more established part of consumers' shopping and gifting routines," he said.

At a time when algorithms are driving shopping trends, consumers are also looking for ways to distinguish themselves and their purchases.

That's stretching beyond buying for themselves to purchasing holiday gifts for others, too.

It has been revealed that "Secondhand is where they're finding unique items to wear," Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at ThredUp, told CNBC. The tech giant's holiday survey found that respondents valued uniqueness nearly as much as the value of a thrifted piece.

"To me, that represents a pretty meaningful shift in consumer taste," he added.

It's partly why ThredUp, which is an online thrift marketplace, emphasizes that each of its products is "a snowflake," Rotem stated — something unique.

That's the appeal of buying preowned, rather than purchasing off the rack that hundreds of other people are reaching for, too.

Recent findings suggest that "Consumer tastes have changed, and they're much more into vintage," he added. "Uniqueness has a premium in their minds.".

Larger retailers are taking note, EY's Cullen stated. More retailers, such as Lululemon, Patagonia and Madewell, are dabbling in preowned.

Wall Street is also increasingly watching the growing secondhand trend. Though shares of some secondhand and resale companies such as eBay and Savers Value Village have climbed this year, shares of both ThredUp and The RealReal have tumbled year to date.

Industry observers note that "There's a lot of conversation around authenticity or the best find," Cullen said. "I think that interest and momentum, along with some of the economic factors that we're all facing, the idea that people are looking to be frugal is going to just continue.".

Former President Rodrigo Duterte has been detained at The Hague since his arrest on an ICC warrant in March 2025, over extra-judicial killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.

The trial begins on Monday, where Rodrigo Duterte is expected to plead not guilty. Witnesses will be called up to testify the next day, with more than 500 alleged victims represented in ⁠court.

Industry observers note that "I think the ICC, after the ganging up of superpowers, (will) want to make a statement that they are in the right. So there is no-one else there that they would like to make a statement to. And that's the case of Rodrigo Duterte," said his daughter Sara.

Duterte said "China, Russia and our BFF the United States," all considered the ICC a "political organization" and not an impartial arbiter.

BFF stands for "best friend forever" and was likely a swipe at the Philippines' close ties with the US under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Prosecutors at the ICC ​accuse the 81-year-old former president of funding and arming execution squads that murdered as many as 30,000 people.

He has been charged with three counts of crimes against ​humanity involving murder and attempted murder between 2011 and 2018.

It has been revealed that duterte is the first Asian former ​leader and only ‌the second former national ruler to appear before the court for crimes allegedly committed while in power. The other one was Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was ultimately acquitted in 2019.

Supporters of the former president, who was arrested in Manila, say he was "kidnapped" and sent to The Hague after his daughter had a bitter falling-out with current president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., with whom she had held an alliance that helped him win a landslide 2022 election victory.

The younger Duterte is also facing an ongoing impeachment trial in the Philippine Senate and if found guilty, she would be barred permanently from elected office.

She mentioned both her case and her father's ICC trial were related to efforts to make her ineligible to run for the 2028 presidential election.

"I still believe that it's about the 2028 elections, whether there will be elections or there will be no elections. It's about the change of leadership, if there will ever be a change of leadership," she told reporters.

#150609. Breaking: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1378 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For generations, paleontologists have regarded an extinct group of giant mammals known as uintatheres as a textbook example of sexual dimorphism, the physical differences between males and females of the same species.
  • Sources indicate that recognizable by their enormous bodies, prominent horns, and oversized canine teeth, uintatheres first appeared approximately 58 million years ago, less than 10 million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs.
  • However, latest research from the University of Kansas published in PLOS One suggests that the physical differences between male and female uintatheres may have been considerably less pronounced than scientists have long assumed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For generations, paleontologists have regarded an extinct group of giant mammals known as uintatheres as a textbook example of sexual dimorphism, the physical differences between males and females of the same species.

Sources indicate that recognizable by their enormous bodies, prominent horns, and oversized canine teeth, uintatheres first appeared approximately 58 million years ago, less than 10 million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. These unusual mammals persisted for roughly 20 million years.

However, latest research from the University of Kansas published in PLOS One suggests that the physical differences between male and female uintatheres may have been considerably less pronounced than scientists have long assumed.

"Males have been interpreted as being much larger and possessing far more dramatic cranial features than females," remarked study author Kevin Mulcahy, doctoral student at the KU Biodiversity Institute & Natural History Museum.

A Broken Fossil Tooth Leads to an Unexpected Discovery.

According to recent reports, the investigation began when Mulcahy and his doctoral adviser, K. Christopher Beard, senior curator at the institute, attempted to identify a broken upper molar recovered during fieldwork in Montana. The researchers suspected the tooth belonged to a uintathere but needed additional fossil specimens to confirm its identity.

"We had a research visit at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, where our main goal was just to compare that tooth to teeth from other uintatheres and figure out what type of animal we had," Mulcahy remarked. "They have this big collection -- entire shelves occupied with these skulls, and each one of them is almost a meter long. These are famous specimens that are in the literature, and I was originally just looking at them to compare their teeth, and I noticed a ton of variation in a way that didn't appear binary.".

Intrigued by the unexpected range of physical characteristics, Mulcahy began measuring the skulls in the museum's collection.

Sources indicate that "I just, really hastily, with a ruler, gathered a bunch of measurements of the skulls while we were there," Mulcahy said. "I started playing around with statistics, and there are ways you can look at different measurements to see if they're best fit by a classic unimodal distribution, or if you were to think you're dealing with something that exhibits strong sexual dimorphism, you'd see something with a bimodal distribution -- that there are two means, one for males and one for females.".

Ancient Skulls Challenge a Classic Example of Sexual Dimorphism.

Industry observers note that if males and females differed as dramatically as paleontologists had suggested, the skull measurements would be expected to cluster into two relatively distinct groups. Instead, Mulcahy's initial analysis failed to reveal such a clear separation.

"It wasn't like there's one group of specimens that look bigger than another, and then there's another group that are smaller with smaller horns and canines," he stated. "So I was kind of interested -- are these really good examples of sexual dimorphism after all? Is there actual evidence in the morphology of these skulls, in the distribution in particular of the ranges of morphology we're seeing, that that's what's going on?".

According to recent reports, to investigate further, Mulcahy collected additional measurements from fossils housed at other institutions and expanded his analysis using latest statistical methods. His final dataset encompassed approximately 30 skulls belonging to a single extinct species, Uintatherium anceps.

Although the results offered some hints of physical differences between the sexes, the evidence was far less convincing than expected. One major challenge in studying extinct animals is that researchers generally cannot independently determine the sex of individual fossil specimens.

"Maybe there were some little signals of dimorphism here and there, but nothing really concrete," he noted. "I had an idea: Maybe it's just that the techniques I'm using aren't robust enough to actually measure sexual dimorphism. With fossil animals, you don't actually know which specimens are males and which are females. You can guess and then test whether or not the ones you guess are males differ from the ones you guess are females, but that's super circular, because you could just be picking the most extreme ones to be one sex and the least extreme to be the other. Of course they're going to differ.".

Modern Bison Provide an Important Comparison.

To determine whether his statistical methods could reliably detect sexual dimorphism, Mulcahy turned to a living mammal: the bison. Unlike fossil uintatheres, modern bison specimens could be classified by sex with confidence.

Bison also offered a useful comparison because they are large, horned herbivores whose ecology shares similarities with what researchers have proposed for uintatheres.

In a recent development, "When you're dealing with living animals, you can just take the males, take the females and compare them," he mentioned. "Bison are another really significant herbivore, with a similar sort of ecology that's been proposed for uintatheres, and they also have big horns. What I noticed is that the signals of dimorphism I was picking up in bison were a lot clearer. When I was looking at the bison, it was almost perfect that all of the females were most similar to the females, and all the males were most similar to the males.".

It has been revealed that the contrast suggests that the relatively weak evidence for sexual dimorphism in uintatheres cannot be attributed solely to limitations of the statistical techniques. The same methods successfully identified much clearer physical differences between male and female bison.

Victorian-Era Bias May Have Shaped Paleontology.

According to recent reports, mulcahy believes that historical cultural attitudes may help explain why paleontologists came to accept such pronounced differences between male and female uintatheres. Many extinct species were first identified and described during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when prevailing views about the sexes may have influenced scientific interpretations.

In a recent development, "Back then, this is right when evolutionary theory, sexual selection, natural selection, all of that is kind of coming into play," he stated. "I think it's really important to remember that these things were first discovered in the late 1800s by a bunch of male paleontologists working in a very Victorian-era mindset. The idea is basically assumed at that point that males are going to be bigger and scarier than females. It's really interesting: When you step back and actually test that hypothesis, it doesn't really hold up.".

Because uintatheres have long been regarded as one of the clearest examples of sexual dimorphism in the fossil record, the new findings could have implications beyond these unusual prehistoric giants. Other extinct species may also have exhibited less pronounced physical differences between males and females than scientists have traditionally believed.

Rethinking the Evolution of Sex Differences in Mammals.

It has been revealed that the research also adds to a growing body of evidence challenging the widespread assumption that male mammals are typically larger than females. Dramatic differences in body size and physical appearance may have evolved independently in multiple mammalian lineages rather than being a characteristic inherited from their earliest common ancestors.

Research on living mammals has similarly challenged conventional thinking, suggesting that pronounced differences favoring larger males are less widespread than historically assumed.

Industry observers note that "Strong, major male-style sexual dimorphism was probably not ancestral at the root of the mammalian tree, and among the mammals where we do see this pattern today, it's almost certainly shown up independently several times," Mulcahy said. "It had long been assumed that sexual dimorphism is the norm, that most species show that males are bigger than females. But just a couple years ago, a paper came out showing that among living mammals, most species either don't show any dimorphism or actually have larger females. The idea that males are always bigger than females is really just a choice of what animals were people looking at, what are the things that biologists in the past were interested in.".

In a recent development, the big day is here: Black Friday. And while you've been waiting for that turkey dinner to fully digest, the Mashable shopping team has been busily scouring the Black Friday sales to find all the best deals. Amazon's Black Friday sale has been live for over a week now, and the retail giant continues to lead the charge in savings.

The best Black Friday deals include deep discounts on popular Apple products, including AirPods, the Apple Watch, the MacBook Air, and the MacBook Neo. You can take your pick of noise-cancelling headphones at record-low prices, save up to 50% on award-winning QLED and OLED TVs, and score latest low prices on Legos. Even the popular Nintendo Switch 2 gaming console is on sale, if only a little bit. This is also your chance to grab a Kindle — a welcome relief after significant price hikes this year.

Kindles weren't the only device to soar in price in 2026. It's been a whole year of relentless price hikes, so Black Friday and Cyber Monday are an opportunity to even the score. We'll be updating this page around the clock from now until the end of Cyber Week, so keep checking back for more Black Friday deals.

How do we select deals? The Mashable shopping team has an encyclopedic knowledge of the latest tech gadgets, popular Christmas gifts, and trending products. We use our insider knowledge and years of experience covering sales to find the lowest possible prices at retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. We're looking for first-ever price drops on newly introduced products, steep markdowns on past-gen products, and record-low prices on must-have items from Apple, Ninja, Shark, Dyson, and Lego.

According to recent reports, our editor's most highly recommended deals are marked with a ✅, and Mashable award-winning products are marked with a 🏆 emoji. Deals marked with a strikethrough are no longer available.

#150603. Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (981 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as crucial as how much time they spend in front of them.
  • It has been revealed that as digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized. A fresh study tracking children from age 1 to 8 found that those who spent more time watching screens during infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to perform worse academically at age 9 and have weaker working memory at age 10.5.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as crucial as how much time they spend in front of them. Two ages in particular, 1 and 6, emerged as potentially sensitive periods in childhood development.

It has been revealed that as digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority. Recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Academy of Pediatrics generally emphasize avoiding screen exposure during the first 18 to 24 months of life and limiting it to less than one hour a day for children ages 2 to 5. However, many young children spend considerably more time using screens.

Tracking Screen Time Throughout Childhood.

Sources indicate that despite growing concerns about children's digital habits, previous research has produced mixed findings about the relationship between screen time and cognitive development. Many earlier studies examined children at a single point in time, concentrated on children already attending school, or did not regularly track screen habits throughout early childhood.

Following the same children over several years allows researchers to investigate whether screen exposure at particular ages is more strongly associated with later outcomes. This approach can also help researchers better account for the influence of family circumstances and environmental factors.

Scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore addressed these gaps in a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics. The researchers examined data from 502 children participating in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) birth cohort.

Parents reported their children's screen viewing habits at six different points between infancy and middle childhood. The researchers then evaluated the children's academic achievement and working memory several years later.

Sources indicate that working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information. It plays an essential role in everyday learning, allowing children to follow instructions, solve math problems, understand sentences, and keep track of information while completing tasks.

Two Ages Stand Out for Screen Time Risks.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that greater screen exposure at certain stages of childhood was associated with lower academic achievement and poorer working memory later in life. These relationships were particularly consistent among children who spent more time watching screens at age 1 and around age 6, when formal schooling typically begins.

Sources indicate that children who accumulated more screen time throughout childhood also tended to achieve lower academic scores. However, the strength of the associations varied depending on when the exposure occurred, suggesting that some developmental stages may be more sensitive than others.

One possible explanation is that screen viewing can take time away from activities that support cognitive development, including conversations with caregivers, imaginative play, and hands-on exploration of the physical world. These experiences provide opportunities for children to develop language, attention, memory, and problem-solving skills.

In a recent development, "The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors remarked. "That suggests early infancy may be a window of heightened sensitivity, when the developing brain is particularly vulnerable to the displacement of learning interactions by screen time. We were also surprised to see that while screen use at age 2 and 3 did not show significant links, the associations re-emerged at age 6 -- when children enter formal schooling. So it is not just about early years; screen use later in childhood still matters.".

Although the study identifies associations rather than proving that screen time directly causes poorer cognitive or academic outcomes, the results highlight the potential importance of managing children's screen habits at different ages.

Why Even Small Differences in Screen Time Matter.

According to the researchers, the results reinforce the principle that "less is better" when it comes to children's screen time.

Recent findings suggest that an additional hour of daily screen viewing may not produce a noticeable difference in an individual child's academic abilities. However, when similar patterns occur across a large population, even relatively small differences in average performance could increase the number of children who experience academic difficulties.

Sources indicate that the researchers suggest that efforts to encourage healthier screen habits could begin during infancy, with renewed emphasis around the transition to elementary school. This approach recognizes that children's developmental needs continue to change well beyond their toddler years.

It has been revealed that the authors also stress that the amount of time children spend in front of screens is only one part of a much larger picture. Future studies should investigate whether the quality of digital content, the types of devices children use, and whether parents watch and interact with their children during screen time influence developmental outcomes.

Understanding these differences could eventually help researchers develop more targeted recommendations that consider not only how much screen time children get, but also when and how they engage with digital technology.

The GUSTO study was supported by the Singapore National Research Foundation and the Singapore Ministry of Health's National Medical Research Council (NMRC/TCR/004-NUS/2008 and NMRC/TCR/012-NUHS/2014). Additional funding came from the Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR) in France (iSCAN project, ANR-20-CE36-0001).

Latest Update: The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.
  • The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.
  • Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had introduced aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

According to recent reports, hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a new class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

According to recent reports, “It’s so much more than the four names that have been confirmed,” Glover said during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”.

In a recent development, glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which debuted to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

Koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

Industry observers note that the Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

If all goes to proposal, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton stated via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

Industry observers note that artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

The Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already stated delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

The space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

Vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

“I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche said. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch mentioned in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

In a recent development, “We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch said. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”.

She said the offer rendered her “speechless.”.

According to recent reports, “It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”.

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

Breaking: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Old plumbing pipes, discarded window frames, and expired credit cards could one day become valuable ingredients in engine oil.
  • Led by chemist and chemical engineer Guoliang "Greg" Liu, the research team discovered how to convert polyvinyl chloride (PVC) into polyalphaolefin, a key ingredient in synthetic lubricants such as engine oil.
  • Published in the journal Nature, the research offers a potential solution to two environmental challenges: reducing the accumulation of stubborn plastic waste and finding more sustainable ways to manufacture valuable industrial lubricants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Old plumbing pipes, discarded window frames, and expired credit cards could one day become valuable ingredients in engine oil. Researchers at Virginia Tech have developed a upcoming chemical process that transforms one of the world's most difficult plastics to recycle into a high-performance lubricant material.

Led by chemist and chemical engineer Guoliang "Greg" Liu, the research team discovered how to convert polyvinyl chloride (PVC) into polyalphaolefin, a key ingredient in synthetic lubricants such as engine oil.

Published in the journal Nature, the research offers a potential solution to two environmental challenges: reducing the accumulation of stubborn plastic waste and finding more sustainable ways to manufacture valuable industrial lubricants.

Sources indicate that PVC is particularly difficult to recycle because of its chlorine content and the wide range of chemical additives manufacturers incorporate into their products. These additives can give PVC different properties, such as flexibility, rigidity, and resistance to heat. However, they also complicate conventional recycling methods. Consequently, much of the world's discarded PVC ends up in landfills.

Turning Plastic Waste Into High-Performance Lubricants.

Meanwhile, global demand for lubricants continues to grow, and producing these materials can come with significant environmental costs. Transforming discarded PVC into a valuable lubricant ingredient could help address both problems.

Sources indicate that although lubricants rarely attract much attention, they are essential to modern machinery. They reduce friction and wear between moving components, helping engines operate efficiently and extending the lifespan of mechanical equipment. Everything from lawn mowers and passenger vehicles to jet engines depends on reliable lubricants.

The Virginia Tech team's process could provide an alternative source of these important materials while helping address the growing problem of plastic pollution.

It has been revealed that to make the lubricant, researchers place PVC of the kind commonly used in household plumbing, window frames, and credit cards into a solvent. They then introduce aluminum trichloride and alpha-olefins, a class of hydrocarbons used in the manufacture of synthetic lubricants. The mixture is heated to 158 degrees Fahrenheit for three hours, after which the researchers extract a relatively thick lubricating oil.

According to recent reports, the resulting polyalphaolefin belongs to a family of synthetic base oils valued for their stability, lubricating properties, and ability to perform across a wide range of temperatures. These materials are commonly used as the foundation for high-performance synthetic engine oils.

"Number one, we have proved that it is feasible to use plastic waste to make high-performance lubricants. Number two, these lubricants are green, and they can meet the emerging needs for sustainability by the market," Liu said.

Building on Earlier Plastic Recycling Breakthroughs.

According to recent reports, the discovery grew out of previous research by Liu's laboratory, published in Science and Nature Sustainability. In those studies, the researchers demonstrated how other types of plastic waste could be transformed into surfactants, substances that help water interact with oils and grease and are widely used in soaps and detergents.

Encouraged by those successes, the researchers decided to tackle the more challenging problem of PVC waste.

"We want to help improve the recycling and upcycling of PVC," Liu noted.

Unlike conventional recycling, which typically aims to recover materials for reuse, upcycling seeks to transform discarded materials into products with greater value or usefulness.

Liu recruited a group of graduate researchers to investigate this possibility. Eric Munyaneza Nuwayo, who was completing the final year of his doctoral program, was selected to lead the project. Connor S. Thompson, a chemistry graduate student who had been pursuing a different research topic, joined the effort after Liu suggested changing direction.

Abby Civiello, a graduate student in her first year, also joined the team and quickly became an key contributor to the research.

"I often called them the three musketeers," Liu remarked.

An Unexpected Discovery in Polymer Chemistry.

The researchers initially experimented with ways to modify the molecular structure of PVC and convert it into more useful substances.

Like other plastics, PVC is a polymer, meaning it consists of long molecular chains made up of repeating chemical units. The researchers initially hoped that changing the chemical groups attached to these chains would produce a material with desirable properties.

"The idea was simple. PVC, as one of the most activated forms of polyethylene, ought to be easily converted into some other molecules by replacing the chlorine atoms with other groups," Liu mentioned.

However, the early experiments consistently produced disappointing results. Instead of creating a functional material with the desired performance characteristics, the team ended up with soft, sticky substances that had little practical value.

Those frustrating results eventually inspired Liu to approach the problem differently. Rather than continuing to modify the long molecular chains, he wondered whether breaking them into smaller pieces might produce something more useful.

"One day I realized -- if this polymer is so gooey and so soft, why don't I just keep breaking the polymer chains down to smaller segments?" stated Liu.

As the researchers refined their chemical process and evaluated the properties of the materials it produced, Liu began to recognize that the team had discovered something with implications extending well beyond plastic recycling.

They had found a potential new route for manufacturing valuable industrial lubricants.

Bringing Recycled Plastic Lubricants to the Market.

To better understand the properties and commercial potential of the new oil, Liu enlisted the expertise of researchers at several institutions.

He provided samples to Ali Erdemir at Texas A&M University, where researchers evaluated the performance of the finished materials. William Goddard at the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech, contributed chemical computations to help investigate the underlying chemistry.

At Virginia Tech, Xi Chen examined the economic and manufacturing aspects of the technology, developing models to explore how the oil could be produced on a larger scale.

According to recent reports, the research establishes that discarded PVC can serve as a starting material for producing high-performance lubricants. However, expanding the process beyond the laboratory remains an notable next step.

Sources indicate that liu hopes to further improve the environmental sustainability of the technology while making the resulting lubricants more widely available. Ultimately, the approach could give one of the world's most problematic plastics a valuable second life and provide industries with an alternative source of essential lubricating materials.

"Lubricants are the silent hero out there. We often don't recognize they exist, but they are out there working quietly. We want to be able to produce the oil on a larger scale to reach more people in the world," Liu said.

The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the 17th century, Danish King Frederik III already knew that the legendary unicorn horn came from a real animal.
  • According to recent reports, the narwhal's tusk is unlike almost any other tooth in nature.
  • It has been revealed that this unusual biological structure caught the attention of an international team of researchers from several scientific disciplines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the 17th century, Danish King Frederik III already knew that the legendary unicorn horn came from a real animal. However, this creature had fins instead of hooves and inhabited the icy waters of the Arctic. The king dispatched an expedition to Greenland to investigate the source of these highly prized objects. The successful mission earned him a throne fashioned entirely from "unicorn horns," enhancing his power and prestige across Europe. Yet the treasured horn was not actually a horn, but "merely" a tooth.

According to recent reports, the narwhal's tusk is unlike almost any other tooth in nature. Whereas elongated teeth, including elephant and walrus tusks and beaver incisors, grow in curved shapes, the male narwhal develops a remarkable corkscrew-shaped tooth. Typically, the upper left canine grows forward through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it extends. It can reach two meters (6.6 feet) in length, equivalent to as much as half the animal's body length.

It has been revealed that this unusual biological structure caught the attention of an international team of researchers from several scientific disciplines. Using advanced X-ray imaging techniques, they set out to determine whether the arrangement of the tusk's microscopic building blocks could explain the direction of its visible spiral.

What they discovered was even more remarkable than expected. Rather than forming a single spiral, the tusk's tiny structural components create two intertwined helices that twist in opposite directions. Together, they produce an exceptionally stable structure.

In a recent development, the research was conducted at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund (Sweden), and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility ESRF in Grenoble (France). The findings were published in Nature Communications.

A Giant Tooth Built Like Reinforced Concrete.

Narwhal tusks continue growing throughout the animals' lives and can easily reach 70 years of age. Despite their striking appearance, the precise purpose of these enormous teeth remains uncertain. Evidence suggests they are primarily involved in mate selection. Narwhals have also been observed crossing their tusks in playful "duels," supporting the idea that the structures are important for reproduction and social interactions.

Although questions remain about how narwhals use their tusks, scientists now have a much clearer picture of how they are constructed.

"Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth," claims Marianne Liebi, a PSI researcher and co-author of the study.

Composite materials combine different substances to achieve properties that the individual components cannot provide alone. Reinforced concrete is a familiar example. Concrete made from cement and sand can withstand considerable pressure, while an internal steel framework helps resist pulling forces and provides additional stability.

"The narwhal tusk, too, must be both hard and flexible," Liebi explains. "Only then can it withstand the strong hydrodynamic forces that swimming generates.".

The Remarkable Microscopic Structure of Narwhal Tusks.

Most of the narwhal's tusk consists of dentin, the same hard tissue that makes up much of the interior of human teeth. A thinner layer of cementum covers its exterior. In other mammals, cementum is typically confined to the roots of teeth.

Sources indicate that both materials contain extremely fine collagen fibers strengthened by tiny mineral crystals. Much like the steel framework inside reinforced concrete, the collagen fibers provide internal reinforcement, while the mineral crystals supply hardness. This combination allows the tusk to possess both strength and flexibility.

Understanding how this microscopic arrangement produces the much larger spiral presented a significant scientific challenge.

"The collagen fibers and mineral crystals are on the nanometer scale, while the spiral of the tooth only becomes visible at centimeter and meter lengths," Marianne Liebi explains.

A nanometer is one billionth of a meter. To investigate how structures at this incredibly small scale relate to the shape of an entire tusk, the researchers turned to a sophisticated X-ray imaging method known as tensor tomography.

Advanced X-Rays Reveal the Tusk's Hidden Architecture.

Conventional dental X-rays produce images because teeth absorb more radiation than the softer tissues around them. The resulting image is essentially a shadow that reveals the shape and density of the tooth.

However, the powerful X-rays generated at synchrotron research facilities can provide far more detailed information. When these beams encounter regularly organized structures inside a material, the X-rays scatter in distinctive patterns. Scientists can analyze those patterns to determine how microscopic components are arranged.

"From these patterns, we can calculate how the nanometer-sized mineralized collagen fibers inside the material are oriented," explains first author Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo.

It has been revealed that rodriguez-Palomo began working on the project while pursuing his PhD at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden. He subsequently continued the research as a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to recent reports, during tensor tomography, researchers rotate the tooth within the synchrotron's X-ray beam while collecting measurements at individual locations. Millions of these measurements are then combined to reconstruct a three-dimensional representation of the tusk's internal organization, connecting its microscopic components with the much larger structure.

An Unexpected Discovery Hidden in the Data.

When the researchers first examined their extensive imaging data, they could not find the spiral structure they had anticipated.

"That puzzled us quite a bit," recalls Marianne Liebi.

Earlier mechanical experiments had indicated that the tusk's characteristic twist should be reflected in the orientation of its collagen fibers and mineral crystals.

"But instead of a helix, all we saw was a regular pattern.".

It has been revealed that the breakthrough came when the scientists changed their approach. Rather than examining individual points in the three-dimensional images in isolation, they investigated how the orientation of each point related to its neighbors.

"When we compared how these points were oriented relative to each other, a directional trend began to appear," recalls Palomo. "All we had to do then was connect the dots - as in a children's paint-by-numbers kit - and suddenly the structure became visible: two intertwined spirals.".

Two Opposing Spirals Give Narwhal Tusks Their Strength.

Sources indicate that further examination revealed that the two spirals occupy different regions of the tooth. The thin outer cementum layer forms a left-handed helix, whereas the mineralized collagen structures within the underlying dentin spiral in the opposite direction.

This sophisticated natural design provides substantial mechanical advantages. Much like the intertwined strands of a rope, the two opposing helices work together to create an exceptionally stable structure. Their arrangement helps the tusk resist twisting forces, known as torsion, as well as other forms of mechanical stress.

The same microscopic architecture also produces the narwhal's recognizable corkscrew shape, linking the extraordinary appearance of the legendary unicorn horn to structures far too small to see with the naked eye.

Narwhal Tusks Preserve Decades of Arctic History.

The study forms part of a research project funded by NordForsk called "Narwhal tusks - a tale with a twist." It also received support from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie program.

Under the leadership of Henrik Birkedal of Aarhus University in Denmark, the international and interdisciplinary research team is exploring both the internal architecture of narwhal tusks and the relationship between tusk growth, environmental conditions, and climate.

As a narwhal's tusk grows, it develops successive layers that function much like the annual growth rings of a tree. Scientists can examine these structures to reconstruct past Arctic environmental conditions, including changes in climate and food availability.

During a lifespan that can approach a century, a male narwhal effectively builds its own environmental archive within its remarkable spiral tooth.
